“Prince Mydeimos, may I speak with you?”

The voice slithered through the dimly lit hallway just as Mydei was making his way back to his quarters after dinner. He stopped, turning to find a tall, slim man leaning just a step too far out of the shadows. The stranger’s attire was immaculate, tailored to an almost theatrical precision, but what unsettled Mydei most was the mask—polished bone-white, covering half his face like a phantom.

Mydei’s brow furrowed. In all his years within the palace walls, he had never once seen this man among the staff, guards, or advisors. “Who are you?” His voice was cool, cautious, though every nerve in his body was on alert.

The man bowed low, fluid, rehearsed. “Forgive me, Your Highness. I should have introduced myself sooner. I am the Queen’s Theoros… Lygus.” His tone was smooth, cultured, but there was something too measured in the way he spoke—like every word had been practiced in a mirror. “If you would grant me a moment, I have something important I must show you.”

The corridor was silent save for the faint hiss of the torches on the walls. Not a guard in sight. Convenient. Too convenient. Mydei’s gut twisted. Everything about this meeting screamed of calculation, of orchestration. And yet, there was that instinct—that strange, unshakable pull—that urged him to follow, as though fate itself was daring him forward.

“My mother’s Theoros?” Mydei murmured under his breath, but he gave a short nod. “Lead the way, then.”

Lygus’s eyes glinted behind the mask, though his smile remained faint, unreadable. He turned with a sweep of his coat and began guiding Mydei down the palace hallways. They twisted through turns that Mydei had walked countless times before, yet somehow, under Lygus’s guidance, the familiar halls felt foreign—narrower and darker.

At last, they reached the doors of the royal library. Mydei’s steps slowed, his chest tightening. The air here was colder, heavier with the scent of parchment and old stone. The library was sacred—its shelves filled with texts preserved by his family for generations. Access was restricted to family and a select few scribes. No servant, no advisor, should have had the key.

Yet Lygus pushed the great doors open without hesitation, as though they had always belonged to him.

Mydei’s eyes sharpened. He stepped inside warily, the silence of the room pressing around him, shadows stretching long between the shelves. The place felt too empty, too still.

He turned, his voice low, demanding. “Speak. Why have you brought us here?”

Lygus closed the doors behind them with a soft click. The sound echoed louder than it should have in the vaulted chamber. He lingered there for a heartbeat longer, his masked face unreadable, before stepping forward with the calm composure of a man who already knew how this would play out.

“Are you familiar with the story of the hero of Aedes Elysiae?”

Mydei froze, caught off guard by the question.

“…What?”

Lygus’s gloved hands moved with eerie calm as he slid a heavy tome from the shelf. The leather cover creaked, dust rising faintly in the air as he opened it. His fingers lingered on an illustration—an old, faded painting of a boy with sharp features that bore a striking resemblance to Phainon. Beside him stood a girl with short pink hair, their expressions hopeful, radiant. At their feet lounged a ginger cat and a fluffy white dog, animals Mydei had seen with his own eyes in Aedes Elysiae.

A cold knot tightened in his stomach. He already sensed where this was leading.

“A long, long time ago in Aedes Elysiae,” Lygus began, his voice unhurried, as though savoring each word, “there lived a boy named Khaslana. From birth, he was told he was destined to be a hero. At first, he didn’t understand what that meant… until he began to remember. Not just his own childhood, but lifetimes—endless cycles—of sacrifice. He had saved Amphoreus time and time again from ruin.”

The name rang strange and familiar all at once, a phantom echo slipping across Mydei’s tongue before he even realized he was mouthing it silently: Khaslana. He had never heard it before. And yet… the weight of it pressed heavily on his chest.

His eyes darted back to the painting. The resemblance was undeniable. It wasn’t just similar—it was Phainon. Or perhaps… Phainon was Khaslana.

Lygus’s lips curled faintly, the kind of smile that revealed nothing but promised everything. He turned another page, revealing twin depictions of Aedes Elysiae. One glowed with vibrancy—lush gardens, bright skies, life flourishing in every corner. The other was its shadow: the same city, but hollowed, decayed, and drowned in ruin.

The silence between them grew thick, the flickering lamplight casting long, sinister shadows across the open book. Mydei’s pulse quickened. His instincts screamed that he had stepped into something far more dangerous than a tale from the past.

“Even though he was a hero across countless lifetimes, he never achieved what he truly longed for,” Lygus continued, his voice low and measured, carrying an almost theatrical weight. “A world where he could reunite with his friends and live peacefully. So his companion, Cyrene, took it upon herself to intervene. She wielded the power of Oronyx to thrust him into the present. But such a feat came at a cost—it drained Aedes Elysiae of its essence, leaving it in ruin.”

Mydei’s gaze lingered on the image of the desolate city. His throat tightened. It matched Cipher’s words perfectly—Aedes Elysiae wasn’t supposed to be thriving anymore. The truth was in front of him, etched in fading ink. Yet the other illustration pulled at him more strongly: the gardens brimming with color, the statue of Oronyx standing tall and unbroken. He could almost make out familiar figures in the painted crowd —Pythias, and even the children he had met.

But Cyrene… that name snagged in his thoughts like a thorn. Phainon had only mentioned her briefly—an old friend, a co-star in a film. Childhood friends, he’d said. The way Lygus spoke, however, painted a far different picture. In this story, Cyrene hadn’t joined Phainon in the present at all. She had given everything—her life, her power—to send him forward.

So what did Phainon mean when he said tabloids had unearthed childhood pictures of him and Cyrene?

The contradiction gnawed at him. Was that story a fabrication? Had Phainon lied to him outright? Or—worse—was he the only one left in the dark about Phainon’s true nature?

Lygus turned another page, the sound of parchment rasping like a whisper in the silent library. His expression didn’t change, but his eyes glinted with something that set Mydei’s pulse racing.

“Khaslana woke in this present age, utterly alone. But he did not arrive empty-handed. He carried with him two relics—two books unlike any other.” Lygus’s voice dropped lower, as though the shelves themselves were listening. “One could bend the fates of his dearest companions, the Chrysos Heirs. The other… would guide him to a man destined to help him accomplish his final wish.”

The words struck Mydei like a blow. His chest tightened, air refused to fill his lungs.

He couldn’t breathe.

The more Lygus spoke, the more the pieces fell together in a grotesque picture Mydei didn’t want to see. Phainon—no, Khaslana—had always been steps ahead. The compass that never failed to point him toward Mydei. The way he seemed to know Mydei’s thoughts before he voiced them. The inexplicable familiarity, the strange certainty in his gaze when they first met.

It had never been chance.

Mydei’s stomach turned. From the very beginning, Phainon had carried the memories of countless versions of him, lived and discarded like pages in a book. Which meant—this was not a love built in the present. This was a script Phainon had rehearsed millions of times over, until Mydei inevitably fell into place.

The realization clawed at him. The tenderness, the whispers in the dark, the confessions he had believed were raw and real—had they all been orchestrated? Had Phainon simply known exactly which words would break down his defenses?

Oh.

A sick, hollow sound escaped him before he could stop it. His chest constricted, cold sweat clinging to his palms.

“Just what might that goal be?” he asked, though his voice wavered, brittle as glass.

“To reset the world.”

The words landed heavy, final.

“Why would he do that?” Mydei whispered, as though the answer itself might undo him.

“Because if he resets the world,” Lygus said smoothly, like a man savoring each cut of the knife, “he could bring back Aedes Elysiae. He could restore Amphoreus to an age where magic thrived, where the Chrysos Heirs would bow beneath his command. A perfect world, designed by his own hand.”

Mydei’s mind reeled. Reset the world? He didn’t even understand what that meant—only that it was cataclysmic, irreversible. Was it truly power that Phainon wanted? Or was Phainon doing it for Cyrene, the girl who had sacrificed herself for him? The thought twisted like barbed wire around his heart.

But one thing was undeniable: Phainon was not merely a man. He was something far greater—and far more dangerous.

“You are lying,” Mydei said, though the words tasted of desperation. “He wouldn’t—he wouldn’t do that.”

“And yet,” Lygus countered, his masked face unreadable, “has he ever told you the truth? Has he ever spoken of where he came from? He has already met you more than thirty-three million times across lifetimes without number. Thirty-three million, Prince Mydeimos. And you were just one more.”

The taunt slithered through the silence, suffocating him.

Mydei staggered back a step, the world tilting beneath him. Thirty-three million lifetimes? He tried to breathe, but the air was thick, cloying. Every memory with Phainon—every glance, every touch—suddenly blurred into uncertainty. Was it ever real? Or had Phainon known exactly how to play him from the moment they met?

Terror swelled in his chest, mingled with a betrayal so sharp it made his eyes sting. He could no longer tell if the ground beneath him was solid—or if he had been standing on a stage built by Phainon all along.

“Shut up.” Mydei roared, his voice cracking down the marble hall, raw and trembling. “Why should I trust you? You don’t even know what I’ve been through—what he and I have—why are you even telling me all this?”

The words spilled out like broken glass, jagged and uneven. His hands balled into fists at his sides, shaking with an anger that couldn’t decide if it wanted to collapse into grief or ignite into violence.

Lygus stood perfectly still, as if the storm before him was nothing more than a passing breeze. “As the Theoros, my duty is to observe,” he said, his voice calm—almost soothing, which only enraged Mydei further. “And I have been observing you for a very long time. I do not lie, Prince. I only record, and report. Understand this: I can ensure he does not reset the world again—as long as I have the book. But if he succeeds, you will lose everything. Your family. Your friends. Your kingdom. Perhaps even your own existence. And your family…”

A pause. Deliberate. Cutting.

“…may suffer a fate far crueler than the one you already know.”

Something in Mydei snapped, and a sharp, almost hysterical laugh escaped him. It rang hollow in the cavernous library, echoing off the shelves of ancient tomes. “You speak like you know my grief,” he said bitterly, his smile twisted, eyes wide and glassy. “Then tell me, all-seeing Theoros. Tell me who killed Hephaestion. Tell me, and maybe I’ll believe a word that drips from your cursed mouth.”

For the first time, the mask seemed to tilt—not in hesitation, but in faint amusement. Lygus’s lips curled, not quite a smile, not quite a smirk. He was utterly unfazed, standing like a figure carved from shadow and stone.

“Very well,” he said smoothly, each syllable deliberate. “The queen did it.”

The words landed like a blade thrust between Mydei’s ribs.

His vision blurred. His breath caught sharp in his throat. For a moment, he forgot how to move, how to think. Then—

“ Blasphemy ,” he hissed, his voice strangled with fury. His eyes burned, and his jaw trembled with the effort to hold himself together. “You dare—”

“If you don’t believe me,” Lygus cut in, calm and unyielding, “ask her.”

The air between them stretched thin, suffocating. Mydei’s pulse thundered in his ears, hot blood rushing in waves of disbelief, rage, and a hollow fear that maybe—just maybe—Lygus was telling the truth.

Lygus’s gaze never wavered. His composure was infuriating, his certainty absolute, as though the chaos tearing Mydei apart was little more than a spectacle he had anticipated from the start.

Mydei’s body moved before thought could catch up. His hand shot forward, seizing Lygus by the collar of his coat, and slammed him against one of the towering shelves. The books rattled from the impact, dust shivering loose from the wood.

“Listen here you bastard,” Mydei spat, his voice breaking between fury and despair. His eyes blazed, but beneath the fire was a glimmer of fear. “If you so much as breathe without telling me first, if you so much as lift a finger without me knowing, I will hurt you. Do you understand me?”

For the first time, the mask tilted back, and Lygus’s mismatched eyes— cold, steady—met Mydei’s up close. Unfazed. Still maddeningly calm.

“I understand,” Lygus said simply, as though Mydei’s threat was nothing more than a detail to be logged in some invisible ledger. His voice was low, almost amused. “But you should ask yourself, Prince… do you truly wish to know the answers you demand?”

Mydei’s grip trembled, nails digging into the fabric, before he shoved Lygus back hard and released him. His breathing was ragged, each inhale sharp like it scraped down his throat.

Without another word, he turned on his heel and stormed out of the library, the heavy doors slamming shut behind him.

The corridors seemed colder now, emptier, as if shadows followed him at every turn. His chest heaved with unspent rage, but beneath it sat something far worse: doubt. The name Khaslana. The ruined Aedes Elysiae. The queen. His mother.

Could any of it be true?

He found himself heading towards the medical wing where Hephaestion's body was, his hands still shaking. He sank into the chair by the window, staring blankly at the night sky beyond the glass. Lygus’s words echoed endlessly in his head, each one gnawing at the fragile seams of his trust. Had he been nothing more than a piece on someone else’s board this entire time?

And worse, if his mother had killed Hephaestion, then what truth had his entire life been built upon?

Then, as if the titans above had heard his prayers, there came a knock on his door.

The moment the hands of the clock in Anaxa’s office finally struck midnight, Phainon decided he had enough.

After his encounter with Lygus, Mydei’s chest was still burning with anger, his thoughts heavy and fractured. He needed air. He needed silence. And so, without realizing where his feet carried him, he found himself in the medical wing.

The room was dim, lit only by a single lantern that flickered against the walls. At the center lay Hephaestion’s coffin, polished wood gleaming faintly in the dark. Mydei lowered himself into the chair beside it, elbows braced against his knees, hands clasped so tightly his knuckles were pale.

The silence was suffocating.

Every word Lygus had spoken gnawed at him—Phainon, Hephaestion, his mother, the fate of Aedes Elysiae. Lies? Truth? A mixture of both? Mydei didn’t know anymore. His head pulsed with too many questions, none of which had answers. His gaze fell to the coffin. Hephaestion’s stillness felt heavier than stone, heavier than the kingdom itself.

Until—

The sound startled him, sharp against the quiet. His head whipped toward the door, heart pounding, irritation sparking.

It must be Lygus. Of course. Who else would follow him even here? His anger flared hot again, chasing away the ache in his chest. Jaw set, Mydei rose abruptly, storming across the floor, ready to tear into the masked man for daring to intrude again.

But when he wrenched the door open—

The hallway was empty.

Cold air slipped into the room, curling around him like a phantom’s touch. Mydei’s brows furrowed as his eyes darted down the corridor. No shadows moved, no footsteps lingered. Only silence.

Then he noticed it.

Resting on the floor just beyond the threshold was an envelope, sealed with a pale pink wax. His name, Mydeimos, was written across it in unfamiliar handwriting.

His heartbeat quickened.

Mydei’s anger faltered, giving way to unease. He crouched, fingers brushing the letter as though it might vanish—or worse, burn him—if he wasn’t careful.

The door shut quickly behind him with a heavy thud, and he turned the lock, pressing his back against the wood as if to bar out whatever had left the letter there. Mydei swallowed hard, forcing his trembling hands steady as he tore the seal open. Inside, folded neatly, was a single sheet of pink-colored paper. The handwriting was careful, almost too perfect, each curve deliberate, deliberate enough to make the hair on the back of his neck rise.

With hesitant breath, he unfolded the note.

To Mydeimos,

Hi~ I hope this letter reaches you safely.

By the time you read this, I imagine things must feel unbearably heavy. Questions with no answers. Shadows at every corner. You’ve probably even started to wonder who you can really trust.

I don’t expect you to trust me. Not yet. You and I have never met, after all. But you do know me, in a way—through him. He must have told you something, at least a whisper of my name. That’s enough.

Come and meet me at the place where you once called home. If you do, you’ll find the answers you’ve been chasing, the truth even he hasn’t told you.

See you soon~!

“…How am I supposed to make the right choice without sacrifices?” Mydei muttered at last. His voice was low, strained—caught between despair and defiance.

Cyrene tilted her head, studying him as though she had been waiting for that very question. Then, slowly, she shifted closer, her presence warm and oddly steady despite the storm that churned within him. She reached out, lacing her fingers with his. Her touch was gentle, yet deliberate, as though binding him to something unseen.

A soft smile curved her lips—not the cheerful grin he had grown used to, but something quieter, laced with secrets she would not yet speak. Her eyes glimmered with that same unreadable depth, both comforting and unsettling.

“You’re asking the wrong question, Mydei,” she murmured. “There is no path without sacrifice. There is only the weight you are willing to carry… and the truth you are willing to face.”

His throat tightened. “Then how do I know which is right?”

Cyrene leaned closer, the distance between them shrinking until her breath brushed against his ear. “You don’t. Not yet.” Her tone softened to something almost coaxing, like a lullaby. “The answer you seek isn’t written in ink or carved into fate—it lies in what you fear to see. That’s why…”

She squeezed his hands, entwining them more firmly.

“…close your eyes, Mydei. I’ll show you what you need to know.”

-x-

This is the story of the Deliverer.

A man born not of flesh and blood, but of calculation and intent—a weapon scripted into being. In the tale of Amphoreus, he was nothing more than a line of code, a cruel experiment stitched together by unseen hands. His companions, the Chrysos Heirs, were no freer than he was. They were constructs, roles fashioned to shepherd him toward one inevitable end: to become the perfect vessel.

Yet whether written or real, pain does not soften when experienced. To the Deliverer, the anguish of loss, the sting of betrayal, the fleeting joy of love —all of it was real enough to scar.

And so the question lingers: who holds the right to decide what is real… and what is not?

The Deliverer fought against the very one who fashioned his existence. He rose each cycle with defiance, enduring torment after torment. He watched the Chrysos Heirs die before his eyes—friends, family, companions— snatched away, only to return in the next cycle and meet the same end again. Thirty-three million times he bore that weight. Thirty-three million times he pressed forward. And yet, even in the end, he never once stood beneath a dawn sky over Amphoreus.

But through all that unending night, there was a single light.

Mydei.

No matter how many times the Deliverer was broken, no matter how deep he sank into despair, Mydei’s presence remained a constant thread. A voice, a hand, a promise that refused to release him. That unyielding light was the tether that kept Phainon from shattering completely.

For that reason, Phainon would move mountains, burn the heavens, and tear down the very world itself if it meant protecting him.

But fate was merciless. The Deliverer did not reincarnate after the final, "perfect" cycle. His body, weary and spent, dissolved into the core of Amphoreus itself, becoming both its heart and its prison. All memory of him faded into silence.

Cyrene alone escaped—hidden within the folds of a fractured time. Patient, waiting, carrying the ember of remembrance. And with that ember, the story took root once more. Not in the main trunk of the Imaginary Tree, but in a branching thread of possibility, where the tale could yet be told anew.

This gave Phainon a second chance at life, having been brought back by the remembrance as well.

Phainon, however, returned incomplete. He no longer carried the same overwhelming power as before, only fractured remnants of who he once was. Pieces of memory lingered—faces of the Chrysos Heirs, fleeting images of battles fought, the echo of promises made. Yet whole chapters of his existence were missing: the truth of Lygus, the terrible sacrifices he had endured for the Heirs, the abilities of the book—or rather, the scepter—all of it lost to the void.

But the recreation of Amphoreus was never without consequence. If every corner of the world had been copied into existence, then so too had its original creator. Zandar could not be erased entirely; his shadow was bound to return, stripped of his former omnipotence yet still bearing the same twisted intent.

Cyrene had foreseen this. That was why she devised her plan—a scheme that stretched across lifetimes, carefully laid like threads of silk over a century. Every step was deliberate, every choice part of a design that would one day give them the chance to defeat Zandar once and for all.

Her plan began with Phainon himself. She tore him free from the inevitability of coreflames, thrusting him into a time where they did not exist. A reality that gave him something he had never known before: the possibility of peace. A life shared with the Chrysos Heirs, unburdened by endless cycles of loss.

But peace demanded sacrifice. Cyrene paid with her life. She drained Aedes Elysiae of its timeless current, burning its power into the charm she carried. Within that azalea bloom, bound by ribbon, she sealed her memories. It would become the key to her reincarnation, the vessel through which she would find her way back into the world.

She believed that fate would lead her to Phainon once more.

And fate did not fail her. When she returned, memory by memory, she found him. And with him, the truth she dreaded. The screenwriter whose name was scattered across the script, the so-called creator of “As I’ve Written,” was Zandar in disguise. The same hand that had once fashioned worlds now shaped them again, twisting destiny into his story.

She chose silence. Phainon had suffered enough, lived through too many endings written in grief. She had sworn that this time, Phainon would have his happiness. If she revealed Zandar’s presence, that fragile dream might collapse before it could even take root.

And yet, promises could only hold so long against the nature of Phainon himself. For though he lived now as a man stripped of divinity, the heart of the hero still beat within him. The same heart that would rather bleed than allow others to suffer in his place.

Cyrene knew that truth too well. She had seen it in every cycle. The thought tightened like a knot in her chest. No matter how carefully she wove her plans, no matter how far she bent the currents of time—Phainon would always walk the road of sacrifice.

In order to create distance between herself and Phainon—and to prevent him from ever suspecting the truth—Cyrene had crafted a scandal. Nothing elaborate, nothing that would crumble her career or draw too much attention, but something simple, sharp, and effective: a dating scandal. Plain enough to be believable, yet devastating enough to push Phainon further from her side. The world whispered, the tabloids spun their tales, and in that noise she found the space she needed to disappear from his orbit.

Over the years, while her name continued to flicker faintly in the entertainment world, she carefully watched from the shadows. She played the part of the distant actress—accepting occasional roles, making just enough public appearances to remain relevant—while in truth, her every move was calculated. Each step, each silence, was designed to keep her unnoticed while she quietly tracked Zandar’s activities. She learned to read his patterns, to map out the trail of his manipulations, even when he was cloaked behind masks of power and respectability.

At the same time, she kept close watch on the Chrysos Heirs. Every rumor, every movement, every strange disturbance tied to their names—she followed it all. She knew that one day fate would stir again, and when it did, she had to be ready.

That day came six months ago. The moment she learned that Phainon had crossed paths with someone new—Mydei—her heart jolted with grim recognition. It was the signal she had been waiting for. Quietly, deliberately, she reached out to Phainon with a casual message, just a few warm words as though no time had passed. True to form, Phainon responded with unguarded joy, eager to hear from her again, utterly unsuspecting of the weight behind her words.

In that moment, Cyrene made her decision.

Mydei who would carry the pen that could rewrite fate. Mydei who would bear the burden of choice. She, meanwhile, would remain the failsafe. The final piece hidden in the margins, ready to act only if everything unraveled and the world began to collapse.

All of that led to this very moment—Cyrene’s cryptic message to Cerydra, the hints about the book, the letter handed to Hysilens—all threads that finally pulled Mydei here. Back to where everything had first begun: his childhood home, walls still faintly echoing with the ghosts of simpler days. And there sat Cyrene, her presence quiet but heavy with intention.

The blue azalea charm resting on the table stirred, a faint golden glow spilling out from its petals as if a heartbeat had awakened within. The light washed over him, and before he could even react, his mind was seized by images—Phainon’s memories, replayed with a clarity so sharp it almost hurt.

The battlefield came first. The cold, suffocating weight of his own titan form, towering and monstrous, and Phainon standing against him. Again and again, Phainon struck him down, only for the cycle to rewind, to replay the inevitable clash. Mydei remembered the pain, but more than that, he remembered Phainon’s eyes—haunted, resolute, breaking a little more with each ending. And yet, through every death, through every reset, his wish to Phainon never changed.

“Deliverer… I wish you… eternal victory.”

The words rang out, unyielding, threaded with defiance and devotion alike. A vow that spanned countless lifetimes.

The memory shifted, softer now. A fleeting moment in the streets of Okehema, his voice casual, almost teasing, but carrying a weight neither of them could ignore.

“If there’s a chance in the next life, you should come visit my library.”

A simple invitation, yet Mydei felt the ache of its unspoken plea: Don’t let me be forgotten.

Then came the last farewell. The moment they both knew would be the end of this cycle, perhaps the end of everything they had fought to keep.

“See you around, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

And Phainon’s reply, unflinching, warm even in its finality.

“It’s a date, Mydeimos.”

The memories weren’t just visions—they were real. Vivid enough that Mydei swore he could feel Phainon’s hand brushing his, hear the lilt of his voice as if he stood in front of him now. For a breathless moment, Mydei thought if he reached out, he might actually touch him.

But then the glow of the charm dimmed, the images dissolving like smoke into the air, leaving behind only silence.

When Mydei opened his eyes, reality returned all at once. He was still in his childhood home, Cyrene watching him quietly. And yet… his face was wet. Tears traced freely down his cheeks before he could stop them. Mydei never cried. Not when he was beaten, not when he was alone, not even when the world seemed too heavy for him to carry. But now—now the grief and love and unbearable weight of Phainon’s story pressed down on him until the tears could no longer be contained.

Cyrene didn’t speak, though a small, bittersweet smile curved her lips. It was a smile that knew sorrow as well as joy, the kind given when words would only break what was already fragile.

For Mydei, the memories lingered like an aftertaste—too vivid, too real to be a dream, yet too fleeting to hold on to. He felt as if he had just awakened from a long, long slumber, carrying with him the undeniable truth: Phainon had left a mark on him so deep that not even time, fate, or the cruel hand of Zandar could erase it.

“I’m sorry I couldn’t save everyone.” Cyrene’s voice trembled, though she tried to steady it with a faint smile. Her fingers tightened around his hands as if holding on to him might ease the weight of her own regrets. “I did whatever I could, but… I wasn’t enough. Now you understand why Zandar must be erased from the story.”

Mydei’s chest constricted at the raw honesty in her tone. For the first time, her ever-playful cheer was gone, replaced by something fragile, almost broken. She had carried this burden far longer than he realized.

His vision blurred, hot tears threatening to fall, but he forced himself to inhale deeply, steadying the chaos inside him. Slowly, deliberately, he wiped his face with the back of his hand. When he looked back at her, his eyes no longer carried only fear—they carried resolve.

He reached for the book, pulling it close, its weight heavier than stone in his lap. The pink-feathered quill glimmered faintly as he picked it up, the feather brushing against his skin like a living thing. He turned to Cyrene, meeting her gaze one last time.

“Thank you… for everything,” he said quietly, his voice steadier now. “I know what I must do.”

Cyrene’s lips parted, as if she wanted to say more, but instead, she only nodded, her expression unreadable—half relief, half sorrow.

And with that, Mydei lowered the quill to the blank page.

The tip touched the paper. Ink spread like veins across parchment.

And Mydei began to write.

5 months later.

The first breath of spring drifted through the half-open window, carrying with it the faint fragrance of new blossoms and the cool dampness of dew. The morning light was soft, golden, spilling across the floorboards in fractured patterns where it passed through the sheer curtains.

Phainon stirred, his body heavy with a weariness that clung like fog. He stretched his arms over his head, joints stiff, a low groan escaping as though he had been asleep for far longer than one night. His chest rose and fell with a deliberate rhythm, almost reluctant to wake, as if part of him still lingered elsewhere.

It felt as though he had wandered through an endless dream—a dream so long it blurred into a lifetime. Yet, as he reached for it, the details scattered like petals in the wind, leaving only the ghost of something important he could no longer grasp. The more he tried to hold on, the more it slipped away, until all he was left with was the dull ache of loss without a name.

With a quiet exhale, he sat up and swung his legs over the edge of the bed, letting his feet press against the cool wooden floor. “...It’s gone,” he muttered to himself, almost as if admitting defeat. Whatever the dream had been, it had left him with only exhaustion.

Deciding not to dwell on it, Phainon pushed himself to his feet and padded toward the washroom. The thought of school—still such an unfamiliar concept in his mind—waited for him like an inevitability. A strange twist of fate had placed him here, in a life where he could rise in the morning, attend classes, and live among others. A life he had once thought forever beyond his reach.

Almost a year ago, he had started attending Okehema University while researching for his upcoming role. The character he was cast to play was a young boy whose ordinary high school life was upended when the world collapsed into chaos. Phainon had never once stepped foot in a public school before; his childhood had been far too sheltered and regimented.

That was why Aglaea, ever practical, suggested he enroll in Okehema University while simultaneously pursuing his history degree. She reasoned that by immersing himself in the routines of school life, he would not only enrich his studies but also breathe authenticity into the boy he was meant to portray.

His agency spared no expense in setting up his living arrangements. They rented him an entire apartment just fifteen minutes from campus—a penthouse that could have belonged to a celebrity twice his stature. From the moment he stepped inside, it felt more like a stage set than a home.

The floors gleamed with polished black marble, streaked with veins of gold that caught the light of the chandeliers overhead. Deep crimson rugs softened the severity of the space, while cushions embroidered with intricate patterns dotted the long leather couches. At night, the city lights spilled across the glass walls, making the entire apartment glitter like a jewel box suspended above Okehema.

The crowning feature, though, was the open-air outdoor bath. It sat nestled on a terrace garden, steam rising in delicate ribbons against the night sky. The first time he stepped into it, he could hear the faint hum of traffic far below while gazing at constellations that seemed almost within reach. It was indulgent, yes—but it was also oddly isolating.

The apartment was supposed to be empty, sterile, untouched by any trace of life beyond his own. But on his second night, he learned otherwise.

A faint, plaintive meow echoed through the darkened hallway as he sat reviewing his notes. Startled, he followed the sound to one of the spare bedrooms. Pushing the door open, he found a calico cat curled up in a patch of moonlight on the floorboards, her fur mottled in hues of cream, amber, and black, with a collar that said 'Meowy'. She blinked up at him with unbothered golden eyes, as though he were the intruder in her space.

No one from his agency had mentioned her. The caretaker swore the apartment had been inspected and cleared before his arrival. And yet, here she was, looking perfectly at home as if she had always lived there.

From that night on, Phainon resigned himself to caring for her. He bought food and toys, learned to deal with her finicky moods, and eventually gave her a name—though he never admitted it out loud to anyone, afraid they might take her away if he grew too attached. The apartment no longer felt like an empty stage; the faint jingle of her collar and the soft thud of paws across marble gave it warmth that no amount of luxury could provide.

However, Phainon couldn’t help but feel like the house was far too big for a person like him to live alone in. The strangest part of all was that neither he nor his management had the faintest clue who the landlord even was. The listing had appeared almost out of nowhere—perfectly timed, as if the place had been waiting for him.

At school, his assigned guide was a man named Caelus—an enigmatic, overly enthusiastic sort who seemed to know far too much about him for someone they had supposedly just met. Caelus was harmless enough, though, his fan-like admiration bordering on comical at times.

Stelle, his twin, was practically a mirror of himself, though infinitely more stubborn when it came to arguments. March, the ever-smiling extrovert, had a talent for making friends with just about everyone on campus. Dan Heng carried a brooding silence about him, his presence familiar in ways Phainon could never quite put into words, like a half-remembered dream.

Hyacine, the Vtuber whose streams occasionally bled into their group chats, was dating Castorice—whose patience with Hyacine’s antics was almost saintly. And Cipher who always lingered at his side like a shadow. Phainon suspected Aglaea had sent him as a watchful guardian, though Cipher never admitted it outright.

Phainon’s group of friends were their own strange constellation of personalities. Yet despite the warmth of their closeness, the laughter, the shared late-night meals and unspoken bonds, Phainon felt a quiet hollowness that none of them could touch. A space inside him that remained untouched, like a note missing from a song. Or rather, not a something… but a someone.

He sighed, grabbing the last of his belongings before heading out. The cool morning air nipped at his face, but it did little to clear the haze of his thoughts. Since it was already near the end of his final semester, there weren’t many classes left to attend. All that really stood between him and graduation was his thesis.

Unfortunately, his last consultation with Professor Anaxa had been scheduled for the earliest slot of the morning. Just his luck.

His thesis focused on the impact of an ancient Kremnoan epic, Odyssey by Gnaeus, on modern culture. Phainon had always been enthralled by Castrum Kremnos and its storied past, though he had never once set foot on its soil. Growing up in Aedes Elysiae, he had heard countless tales of their great hero, the brutal wars, and the endless bloodshed that shaped their identity. The stories painted Kremnos as a land forever scarred by conflict —yet that darkness was precisely what fascinated him. At one point, he had even considered becoming a historian if his life in acting didn’t work out.

“Do you think I should remove the cross-reference to Zandar’s work?” Phainon asked, tapping the margins of his draft where he had underlined the section on radicalization. His brow furrowed in hesitation. “I mean, he made some interesting points, but… honestly, he comes across as too much of an extremist.”

Without sparing even a glance at the paper, Anaxa waved his hand dismissively. “Remove his references. All of them. Whatever that man wrote is drivel—a disgrace to the name of scholarship in Amphoreus.”

Phainon blinked, then laughed awkwardly, trying to soften the edge of the moment. “Yeah… I thought so.”

Anaxa’s reputation was larger than life. A prolific scholar, researcher, and thinker, he had produced seminal works that shaped the field of world history. Students across Amphoreus revered him for his brilliance, while peers respected his sharp insight—even if they feared his equally sharp tongue. His enmity with Zandar, however, was infamous. Zandar had been his rival in academia, publishing works that courted scandal as much as they pursued knowledge.

“Thank Ceres that arrogant philosopher is finally dead,” Anaxa muttered under his breath, the words sharp and venomous.

Phainon nearly choked on his own saliva. He jerked upright, eyes widening.

“P-professor?!” he sputtered, voice cracking in disbelief.

“What?” Anaxa scoffed, leaning back in his chair with a derisive snort. “It’s not like they’ll arrest me for speaking the truth.”

Phainon darted a wary glance around the consultation room, lowering his voice to a whisper. “But what if someone hears you?” His shoulders tensed as though expecting a hidden scribe or spy to spring out from the bookshelves.

“I don’t care,” Anaxa replied flatly, folding his arms. “In fact, I wish I could personally thank the killer myself.” His expression was unflinching, unbothered.

Phainon stared at him, utterly stunned. Though part of him wanted to scold Anaxa for his brazenness, the other part—deep inside—reluctantly agreed. Zandar had produced thought-provoking works, yes, but his arrogance was legendary, his writings laced with self-aggrandizement and veiled contempt for anyone who dared oppose him. He paraded himself as omnipotent, as though he alone bent the world’s truths to his will. It wasn’t just arrogance; it was tyranny in ink.

Five months ago, Zandar had died under mysterious circumstances. Officials had stamped the case as suicide, but whispers in taverns, lecture halls, and private salons all suggested otherwise. Some insisted it was murder, carefully orchestrated. Others claimed he had cheated death entirely, leaving behind a corpse only as a mockery.

Whatever the truth was, most people reacted the same: relief.

Phainon discussed his work with Anaxa for a good two hours before he was finally free. When he glanced at his phone, it was only 11 a.m. His friends wouldn’t even be out of their classes until later in the afternoon, and with no lessons left on his own schedule, there was little point in lingering around campus. After a moment’s thought, he decided to take a walk through Kephale Plaza.

It was strange, almost surreal, how easy it was now to step onto public transport without drawing a mob. When he had first moved into the area, anonymity had been impossible. Even the briefest attempt at a stroll would result in flashes of cameras, microphones shoved in his face, or strangers asking for autographs when he only wanted to buy bread. For a while, it had felt suffocating—he had to disguise himself with masks, hats, even tinted glasses, or else charter private cars just to move around.

But things had shifted over the past eleven months. His management team had worked tirelessly behind the scenes, releasing official statements and gently steering the public away from hounding him. The tabloids, once relentless, found new prey, and the locals gradually adjusted to the idea that a star lived quietly among them. He had become part of the scenery, like the street vendors and thrift stalls—still recognizable, yes, but no longer a spectacle.

Now, aside from the occasional paparazzo lurking at the edge of a square or a passerby sneaking a blurry photo, Phainon could wander as if he were just another face in the crowd. Kephale Plaza welcomed him with its familiar sprawl of old thrift stores, family-run ateliers, and cozy cafés. He slipped into shops without hesitation, buying little trinkets or clothes he had no real need for, chatting briefly with the shopkeepers who had long since stopped treating him like a celebrity. To them, he was just “that young man with a taste for unnecessary purchases.”

After picking up a small bag of snacks for Meowy, his cat, he drifted toward Marmomeal Market, letting the sounds and smells of sizzling food and fresh produce wash over him. The energy was lively but ordinary— comfortingly so.

Passing by a gym called Krateros Vanguards, he slowed for a moment. The fighters inside moved with sharp precision, their muscles honed and intimidating. He remembered once entertaining the thought of joining. After all, he was no stranger to fight training thanks to his acting career. Still, compared to those iron-built physiques, he looked almost average, even frail. With a wry smile, he kept walking.

By the time evening crept in, the sky tinged with shades of red and gold, Phainon had picked up a simple dinner to bring home. The thought of quiet —his own apartment, Meowy curling around his legs, and perhaps some time to read or sketch—was more appealing than anything else.

Just as Phainon had finished showering and was about to eat, his phone pinged. He sat down at his dining table, towel still draped over his shoulders, and glanced at the screen. It was a message from Cyrene—his childhood friend, his sister in all but blood, and an actress who shared the same agency as him.

Cyrene~♪: Cassie and I are arriving tonight~! I hope you have something decent to wear tomorrow otherwise I’ll have no choice but to raid your home.

Phainon rolled his eyes, chuckling as he thumbed a reply.

Phainon: *Hey, what’s that supposed to mean? I always dress decently :( *

A pause, then the typing bubble appeared.

Cyrene~♪: …Somehow that is not assuring at all… Cyrene~♪: Y’know what? We’ll meet tomorrow, 10am at the plaza.

Phainon: Rude?! But sure. We gotta buy some food for the picnic anyways.

He sighed, shaking his head with a grin as he set the phone down. Some things never changed—Cyrene would always tease him for his supposedly “poor” sense of fashion. She wasn’t wrong, though; his other friends often joined in, making it one of those long-running jokes he could never quite escape. Still, he didn’t mind. It was a part of what made her feel so familiar, so grounding, no matter how much time passed.

It had been five months since they had last seen each other in person. Too long, in Phainon’s mind. Between filming schedules, agency obligations, and constant travel, his days had blurred into one another. The thought of seeing her again, of falling back into the ease of their banter, put a warmth in his chest he hadn’t realized he missed until now.

And this time, it wasn’t just Cyrene. His other friends, along with his management team, were all planning to gather in Okehema for the flower viewing festival—a celebration marking the start of spring. Kephale’s court, famed for its sprawling cherry blossoms and vibrant flower fields, would be the heart of the festivities. Food stalls were promised to line the walkways, the air rich with the scent of grilled skewers and sweet dumplings, laughter weaving with music carried on the spring breeze.

Their group chat had been buzzing with excitement for weeks, every detail planned down to who was bringing the picnic mats and who was responsible for the drinks. Tomorrow, they would spread out under a canopy of blossoms, sharing food, teasing one another, and celebrating the fleeting beauty of the first blooms of spring together.

Phainon leaned back in his chair, letting the anticipation settle in. After months of endless work, tomorrow finally felt like a chance to breathe.

He smiled, putting down his phone as Meowy hopped onto his lap.

Tomorrow was going to be a great day.

-x-

When morning came, Phainon practically sprung out of bed, energy thrumming through him like he’d been waiting for this day all week.

He splashed water over his face, ran fingers through his hair, then paused to carefully style it into something neat but not too practiced. Aglaea’s voice lingered in his mind—her reminder about colors—so he stood before his open wardrobe, piecing together the outfit like it was a puzzle.

A black turtleneck layered beneath a crisp white blouse, tailored white pants, and a few gleaming accessories that caught the morning light when he moved. To top it off, a deep blue coat draped elegantly over his shoulders.

He lingered in front of the mirror for a moment, tilting his head, narrowing his eyes. Not bad. Presentable, at the very least.

His gaze drifted to the corner where Meowy lounged lazily on a sunlit patch of floor. “You’re coming with me today,” he announced. The calico flicked her tail, then perked up as if she understood. Phainon rummaged for a sling bag spacious enough, setting it down so Meowy could step in at her own pace. She curled inside, peeking out with curious eyes, the faint rumble of her purr vibrating against the fabric.

The city greeted him with a wash of crisp spring air as he stepped outside. The streets bustled in their usual rhythm—vendors arranging displays, cars weaving through traffic, a faint melody of buskers carried from a nearby corner. Phainon adjusted the strap of his sling and set off toward Kephale Plaza.

By the time he arrived, the plaza was alive with chatter and the shimmer of the fountain at its heart. Blossoms scattered in the breeze, drifting down to float briefly on the water’s surface before sinking. He scanned the crowd until a flash of pink hair caught his attention.

There she was—Cyrene—sitting casually on the fountain’s edge. A short white dress and a violet coat softened the brightness of her pink hair, and she swung her legs idly as though she had all the time in the world. The corners of her lips lifted the moment she noticed him.

Phainon strolled over, his steps quickening despite himself.

“Did you miss me~? How have you been? It’s been a while since we hung out together like this,” Cyrene greeted, her smile bright, eyes carrying that familiar glint of mischief.

Before Phainon could answer, Meowy poked her head out of the sling bag, blinking at Cyrene like she was sizing her up. The sight drew a soft laugh from Cyrene as she leaned forward, hand hovering playfully toward the cat.

“I missed you too, Meowy~!”

Phainon’s heart warmed at the sight of Cyrene scratching under Meowy’s chin. The cat leaned into her touch, eyes fluttering shut in pure contentment, and Cyrene giggled softly, brushing back a lock of pink hair as if she had all the time in the world to devote to coaxing a cat’s purrs. For a moment, Phainon simply watched. The fountain’s spray shimmered in the sunlight, children’s laughter carried across the plaza, and Cyrene looked so effortlessly at ease that it tugged at something deep inside him.

It truly had been a long time since they were able to just be. No handlers. No bodyguards. No flashing cameras or contracts hanging over their heads. The last time he’d seen her—five months ago—it had been a fleeting dinner sandwiched between her press tours. She had flown into Okehema for a night, and their conversation had been rushed, half-eclipsed by the looming awareness that she’d be gone again by morning.

Now, however, the world felt still. She was here. And so was he.

“Of course I missed you,” Phainon said at last, offering his hand to pull her gently up from the fountain’s edge. She took it with that familiar, teasing smile that hadn’t changed since they were merely children in Aedes Elysiae.

“Honestly? I’ve been great. I know attending university was supposed to be research for a role, but… I actually enjoy being a student.”

“That sounds so like you,” Cyrene replied, slipping easily into step beside him as they began to wander the plaza. “Who else would turn a disguise into a lifestyle?” Her laughter was light, but there was warmth in it—the kind of laugh that made his chest ache with nostalgia.

They strolled past flower vendors and shop windows, weaving through the hum of the crowd. Cyrene teased him about his outfit, feigning disbelief that he’d managed to dress himself so well without her intervention. Phainon only rolled his eyes, but secretly, he was glad she noticed.

Their chatter flowed effortlessly, like water over smooth stones, slipping from stories of the sets she’d worked on to his classes, to the mundane and the silly. Every word built a bridge back to the way things used to be— when their friendship wasn’t hemmed in by fame, but alive in the small, ordinary moments.

The scent of something sweet drifted through the air as they turned a corner. A small café, quaint and tucked between larger storefronts, had a signboard out front boasting golden honeycakes, fresh from the oven. Cyrene caught his glance and grinned knowingly.

“You’re thinking it too, aren’t you?”

Phainon chuckled. “You know me too well.”

They slipped inside, the bell above the door chiming softly. Warm air and the buttery fragrance of baked goods enveloped them, chasing away the cool spring breeze. They settled by a window where the sunlight pooled, a small plate of honeycakes between them. The golden crust flaked beneath Phainon’s fork, the sweetness of honey clinging to his tongue. It wasn’t the food, though, that filled him with warmth—it was the company.

He leaned back, watching Cyrene lick a trace of honey from her fingertip, laughing at something Meowy did under the table. In that moment, Phainon felt like life was close to perfect. He had friends who cared, a career he loved, a chance to live as more than just a celebrity.

And yet.

“Lately…” he began, setting his fork down, voice soft against the clink of porcelain and hum of quiet conversation around them. His eyes drifted to the sunlight outside, watching people cross the square. “Lately I’ve been feeling like… something’s missing.”

The words slipped out before he could stop them, leaving the air between them faintly charged, as though the warmth of the café couldn’t quite chase away the chill of that truth.

Phainon chewed the last bite of honeycake slowly, watching Cyrene’s eyes dance as she spoke. She made a soft, encouraging hum—“Hmm?”—with her cheeks still rounded from the sweet, and reached for her cup without taking her gaze off him. Her pink hair fell forward as she tilted her head; she had that easy, teasing look that made confessions feel less heavy.

He folded his hands around his fork, trying to find words. “I don’t know,” he said, voice low enough that it could have been a private thing between them and the hum of the café.

“Something feels a little off. Not in a bad way—” He glanced up, meeting her eyes, and forced a small smile that didn’t quite reach them. “I haven’t had problems with fans or stalkers or anything, but… I guess I do feel a little empty. Sorry, I know that sounds kinda weird.”

Cyrene’s expression softened. She set her cup down with exaggerated care, leaning forward on her elbows as if bridging the space between them physically might help. Her fingers drummed a light, rhythmic pattern on the table—an old habit whenever she was trying to coax someone into speaking more.

“Not at all,” she said. “I told you before that you can tell me anything, and I still mean it.” Her voice was warm, but she didn’t smother him—there was a playful tilt to it, the kind that let him feel safe enough to be honest without feeling pitied. “Do you… feel lonely?”

Phainon let out a short laugh that sounded too brittle to be amusement. He picked at the napkin, tugging the corner between thumb and forefinger.

“Uhhh… maybe? I don’t know.” He shrugged, a small, helpless motion. “Caelus and the gang are all great. We hang out a lot. I visited my folks in Aedes Elysiae before school started. Everything’s—good. I mean, my career’s going well. I’m doing work I like. But… I’m turning twenty-eight this year, and it’s this stupid little voice that keeps whispering I should be doing more. Like finding a partner, settling down, or something meaningful beyond the next role or semester.”

He rubbed the bridge of his nose, eyes flicking to the window where sunlight painted people in hurried, sunlit rectangles. “It feels silly to compare, but sometimes being busy isn’t the same as being fulfilled.”

Cyrene considered him, one eyebrow lifting in that distinctly mischievous way of hers. She balanced the spoon on the saucer then tapped it thoughtfully against the rim, a small, deliberate sound. “Hm.” She let the thought hang between them, then grinned. “What if… I introduced you to someone?”

Meowy, who had been snoozing in the sling by Phainon’s feet, lifted her head at that and gave a sleepy chirp—an approving, if indifferent, seal of feline consent. She circled the bag once and tucked her nose against Phainon’s ankle, anchoring him to the simple, warm reality beneath the anxious thought.

Phainon rolled his eyes and leaned back in his chair, arms folding across his chest. “How are you going to find someone who isn’t my fan and can keep up with my schedule? You realize I barely keep up with my schedule, right?”

Cyrene didn’t even blink at his skepticism. She propped her chin on her palm, watching him with a sly little smirk as though she’d been waiting for him to ask that question. “You underestimate me,” she said, voice lilting with amusement. “I have a friend who just signed under our agency. He’s talented, he’s stable, he happens to be very attractive, and he’s a musician. Basically, tailor-made for you.”

Phainon let out a laugh, covering his mouth with one hand in mock disbelief. “Oh? Does he also happen to be blonde, buff, and built like a god?”

Cyrene’s grin widened until it was positively feline. She sat up straighter, her eyes glittering with mischief as she leaned across the table, closing the space between them. “Are you interested? Because you know I’d only ever recommend the best people for you.” Her tone was teasing, but her gaze held a thread of genuine intent—she really did want to see him happy.

Phainon paused, his playful façade faltering just slightly as he tapped his fork against the rim of his plate. For years, he had dodged these conversations with her. Every time she had suggested someone—co-stars, acquaintances, fellow actors—he had waved her off with excuses: too busy, not ready, not interested. And back then, it had been true. He was buried in roles, constantly chasing the next opportunity.

But now… things were different. His upcoming project was monumental— an entire superhero franchise with a ten-year contract, three solo films already guaranteed. For the first time in his career, he didn’t have to scramble or stress about what came next. There was room to breathe. Room to… maybe, just maybe, let someone else into his life.

He exhaled, a sigh that carried both resignation and relief. “Fine,” he said, pinching the bridge of his nose before looking at her again. “How are we going to do this?”

Cyrene’s eyes widened, then lit up with delight. She slapped the table once with both palms, startling Meowy, who blinked indignantly from her sling. “Really?! Oh, you are going to love him, I promise!” Her voice bubbled with excitement as she fumbled for her phone, nearly knocking her water glass over in her haste. “He’s moving to Okehema soon, so the timing is perfect. I’ll get him to contact you.”

Phainon couldn’t help but chuckle, watching her enthusiasm with a fond shake of his head. She was practically bouncing in her seat, typing furiously into her phone and—he suspected—sending far more messages than strictly necessary. Her glee was infectious, though, and despite himself, he felt a smile tugging at his lips.

“Don’t look so smug,” he teased, nudging her ankle beneath the table with his foot. “If this goes horribly, I’m blaming you.”

Cyrene looked up from her phone, her mischievous grin returning in full force. “Please. When have I ever steered you wrong?” She tilted her head, hair spilling over one shoulder, and gave him a look that made it impossible to tell if she was joking or if she had been planning this all along.

Phainon leaned back, narrowing his eyes playfully. “You’re enjoying this way too much.”

“Of course I am,” she said sweetly, winking as she slipped her phone back into her pocket. “Because this time, I know I’ve got it right.”

While Cyrene typed away furiously on her phone, her thumbs flying across the screen with a speed that suggested she was orchestrating far more than just a single introduction, Phainon glanced at his watch. The café’s sunlight slanted differently now, warmer, and the low chatter around them reminded him they had other plans for the day.

He leaned forward, resting his forearms on the table as Meowy stirred faintly in the sling by his feet. “Anyways,” he said with a soft nudge of his voice, “come on, we gotta go. We still need to pick up those strawberry pastries Hyacine wanted.” He tilted his wrist so the watch caught the light, raising a brow at her.

“Mm, give me a sec—” Cyrene muttered distractedly, eyes still glued to her screen. But at his pointed look, she tapped out one final message with a flourish, the corner of her lips quirking upward in triumph. “Okay, done.” She slipped her phone into her coat pocket, grabbed her glass, and with a dramatic flourish, downed the last of her drink in one go.

Phainon chuckled, shaking his head. “You act like we’re late to a red-carpet premiere.”

“Strawberry pastries are a premiere,” she shot back playfully, standing and smoothing down her dress. “You don’t keep people waiting for those.”

He rose as well, adjusting his coat and slipping the strap of Meowy’s sling more securely over his shoulder. The cat poked her head out sleepily, blinking as if mildly inconvenienced by all the movement. Phainon gave her a gentle scratch between the ears before turning to Cyrene.

She was already at the door, holding it open for him with a grin. “Come on, star boy. Let’s get going before Hyacine starts calling us.”

Phainon rolled his eyes, but the warmth in his chest lingered. Walking past her, he caught the faint scent of her perfume, something light and floral, mingling with the sweetness of honey still lingering on the air. Outside, the plaza had grown busier, the fountain sparkling under the sun, and the energy of the city pressed in around them.

Yet as they stepped out together—her stride light and lively, his more measured but no less content—he couldn’t shake the thought that, for the first time in a while, he wasn’t just moving through his schedule. He was… enjoying it.

Cyrene bumped her shoulder lightly against his arm as they fell into step. “Pastries first, matchmaking later.”

Phainon let out a breath of laughter, glancing sidelong at her mischievous grin. “Right. Pastries first.”

And with that, the two of them slipped back into the rhythm of the plaza, leaving the café—and the sweetness of their conversation—behind.

Phainon’s fingers twitched as she placed it gently into his palm. The charm was cool to the touch, yet it felt inexplicably heavy, as though it bore more meaning than the words she had spoken.

“Did you know that the azalea has many meanings?” Cyrene went on, lifting her own charm—a pale pink azalea that glowed faintly in the light. “It could mean longing for home, or passion and grace. But it also means devotion—love that endures despite the hardships that come along the way.”

Her words lingered in the air longer than they should have, weaving between them in ways he couldn’t quite untangle. Phainon stared at the charm in his hand, brows furrowed faintly. Everyone else’s flowers had felt straightforward, chosen to reflect them in obvious, visible ways. But his? Red didn’t match his eyes, his hair, or even his wardrobe. He never wore the color, never sought it. And yet… something about it fit. He couldn’t explain why, but it settled into him as if it belonged there all along.

“Why is my flower red?” he asked finally, his voice rougher than he intended.

Cyrene tilted her head, her expression unreadable—half playful, half knowing. “Because azaleas don’t come in blue, silly.” Then, after a pause, her tone dipped lower, almost secretive. “But if you do find one… you should hold on to it forever.” She punctuated the words with a wink, as though it were nothing more than a joke, yet her gaze lingered on him a beat too long.

Phainon’s chest tightened, his heart suddenly racing for no reason he could name. A blue azalea? The thought was absurd, but the way she said it— cryptic, certain—lodged itself inside him like a seed waiting to bloom.

He swallowed, forcing a smirk as he rolled his eyes. “I’ll be sure to remember that,” he said, though the words came out softer than he meant them to.

And yet, even as the group’s laughter rose again around them, Phainon couldn’t shake the weight of her charm in his palm, nor the way her final words echoed in his mind.

His thoughts were interrupted by March calling them for a photo. Her voice rang across the picnic spot, bright and insistent, as she waved them over. The tripod was already set up, its little red light blinking, and the rest of the group had squeezed together in a jumble of colors and laughter beneath the cherry blossoms. Cyrene was already jogging lightly ahead, her hair catching the sunlight like threads of silver-gold.

“Get in here, Phai, Cyrene! Let’s take a photo!” March called again, motioning frantically before she dove back into place beside Stelle.

Phainon glanced at the charm one last time, the red azalea gleaming faintly in the casing, as if it wanted to remind him of Cyrene’s cryptic words. With a faint huff, he slipped it into his pocket, the weight of it settling warmly against his side.

He quickened his pace, chasing after Cyrene, who was already laughing as she squeezed between Hyacine and Castorice, tugging them closer for the shot. Phainon took his place at the end, crouching slightly so that the cats— Can, Ica, and Meowy—could be included too, lounging contentedly on the picnic mats in front of them.

“Alright, ready? Say cheese!” March chirped.

The camera clicked, capturing not just their smiles but the flurry of pink petals drifting around them, the gleam of the river nearby, and the overflowing spread of food that spoke of effort and care from everyone present. It was messy, loud, and a little too crowded—but somehow, it felt perfect.

As Phainon straightened, watching the others tease each other and argue over which photo looked best, he felt something stir quietly in his chest. He didn’t know why, but the thought came unbidden, warm and certain.

Somehow, he had a feeling that something good was going to happen.

Perhaps… soon.

In the early hours of Monday morning, Phainon hopped out of bed with an ease that surprised even him. The sunlight had barely spilled past the curtains, soft and golden, yet he felt unusually refreshed. It was almost suspicious—he usually hated Mondays, hated the groggy weight that came with dragging himself out of bed before noon. But today, for some reason, his steps were light.

Maybe it was the weekend still lingering in his chest—the laughter under the cherry blossoms, Cyrene’s cryptic gift, or simply the feeling of being surrounded by friends. Whatever it was, it carried him through his morning routine like a current, and before long, he was out the door with his satchel slung across his shoulder.

“Thesis day,” he muttered to himself, determination sparking. “Let’s get this done.”

He treated himself on the way to campus, stopping by a little café near the school. The warm aroma of roasted beans and buttered pastries welcomed him, and he ordered a large coffee to go, cradling the cup between his hands as though it contained all the motivation he needed.

By the time he entered the university library, the hush of the place wrapped around him like a spell. Sunlight streamed in from the tall windows, dust motes drifting lazily through the beams of light. Rows of books stretched into quiet corners, and the faint scratch of pens or the muted clicks of keyboards blended into the air.

Phainon found his usual spot near the window, set down his bag, and opened his laptop. The screen glowed to life, and he pulled up his thesis file with a sigh. Just one last push, and freedom was his.

He barely began to scroll through his document when the chair across from him scraped softly against the floor. Someone had sat down.

Without looking up, Phainon assumed it was nothing unusual. The library was large but seats filled quickly in the mornings. Probably just another student, maybe even a fan who recognized him but decided to keep quiet. He adjusted his screen, sipping his coffee, intent on ignoring them.

The silence stretched on for several beats, and he felt the faint pressure of eyes on him. The air seemed to shift, subtle but undeniable. Then, at last, the stranger spoke.

“Hey,” the stranger greeted. His voice was dark and smooth, carrying easily across the wooden table—far too bold for the hushed library. “You’re not going to ask for a selfie?”

Phainon blinked, brows knitting. “Huh? Why would I—?”

He finally looked up.

And in an instant, the world tilted.

Blonde hair with crimson tips that caught the morning light like fire. A small braid threaded neatly along one side, deliberate yet casual. Eyes— golden, gleaming, steady, like they had been waiting for him. And a smirk, curved and familiar, as if it had always been meant for him and him alone.

Phainon’s breath caught. His chest tightened. It was like a dam inside him had cracked open, and everything—grief, joy, longing, sorrow, relief— came rushing in at once, too much, too fast. He couldn’t breathe. He knew this man. He knew him in his bones, in the way his heart lurched painfully in recognition, even though his mind screamed that this was impossible.

“You—” His voice broke.

The stranger leaned back in his chair, unbothered by Phainon’s trembling. “You may call me Mydeimos.”

The name slid into Phainon like an arrow. Mydeimos. Mydei. It stirred something deep, tugged at threads he couldn’t see but felt. He pressed a hand over his chest as tears spilled hot and sudden down his cheeks, startling even himself.

“I—” His words tumbled uselessly, breath shuddering. “Why… why do I— why does it feel like—?” He buried his face in his palms, shoulders trembling. He didn’t understand. He had no memories, no context, no reason to feel like this. Yet seeing this man sitting across from him filled him with so much raw emotion it was unbearable.

Mydei watched him quietly, golden eyes softening. There was no surprise in his expression, no confusion—only a calm patience, as though this was exactly how things were meant to unfold. He didn’t reach across the table, but his presence alone was grounding, steady, like a weight that anchored Phainon against the tide threatening to pull him under.

Phainon lowered his hands, his cheeks wet, his lips trembling as he tried to steady his breathing. His fingers dug into the fabric of his pants under the table, grounding himself on something tangible. “I’m sorry,” he whispered hoarsely, though every beat of his heart screamed otherwise. “I don’t know what came over me. You just… you seem so familiar. Have we met somewhere before?”

Golden eyes lingered on him, steady and unflinching. Mydei’s smirk softened, but his gaze held a weight that made Phainon’s chest ache. Every second of silence felt purposeful, as though Mydei was choosing— deliberately—what truths to share and what to conceal.

“Maybe,” Mydei finally said, voice smooth but laced with something unspoken. “In a different timeline or something.”

Phainon’s breath hitched again, his brows knitting. He laughed weakly, though the sound cracked under the tension in his throat. “A… different timeline? That’s—” His voice faltered. “That’s ridiculous.” But the way his chest tightened told him it wasn’t.

He shifted in his seat, desperately trying to compose himself, swiping at his damp cheeks with the back of his hand. He wanted to look normal, unshaken, but he couldn’t hide the way his body leaned unconsciously toward the man across from him, as if drawn by some invisible thread.

“Wait…” Phainon’s eyes narrowed, searching Mydei’s expression for something—anything—to make sense of this. “Did Cyrene send you here? Are you the musician she was talking about?”

The corner of Mydei’s lips curled ever so slightly, as if he’d been expecting that question. “Perhaps.”

The answer was maddeningly vague, and yet the way he said it—low, deliberate, with his gaze never leaving Phainon’s face—made Phainon’s pulse skip. Mydei spoke with a calm certainty, like every word was measured, like he knew exactly how fragile Phainon’s heart was in that moment.

Phainon swallowed hard, unable to break free from that golden stare. He didn’t understand it, couldn’t name it—but beneath the confusion, beneath the ache in his chest, there was an overwhelming warmth. A feeling of being seen. Of being recognized.

And it scared him.

“What are you working on anyways? Aren’t you graduating soon?” Mydei asked casually, shifting with the ease of someone who belonged everywhere he sat. Without waiting for permission, he moved around the table and settled right beside Phainon, leaning over to peer at the glowing screen.

Phainon went rigid. Every instinct told him to edge away, to put some space between them—but he didn’t move. Couldn’t. Mydei’s cologne carried faint hints of sandalwood and pomegranate, grounding yet intoxicating, and the warmth of his shoulder brushing against Phainon’s arm sent sparks racing down his nerves. His fingers hovered uselessly above the keyboard, forgotten.

“Y-Yeah, uh… I just have to submit my thesis,” Phainon stammered, his voice cracking slightly. He prayed Mydei wouldn’t notice the pink burning up his cheeks.

“Boring,” Mydei drawled, his smirk widening just enough to make it sting —but not cruelly.

“...Well, excuse me for trying to complete my education,” Phainon muttered defensively, trying to refocus on the words on his screen, though they swam out of meaning under the weight of golden eyes watching him.

“Can we go back to your apartment or something?” Mydei asked suddenly, his tone smooth, almost playful, though his gaze locked with Phainon’s as if testing him. “You can work on your thesis there and I’ll… cook you food.”

Phainon blinked, lips parting soundlessly. Cook me food? He was still reeling from the way Mydei had slipped so easily into his personal space, and now this stranger—this dangerously handsome stranger with his braid and burning gold eyes—was asking to step into his home.

It was insane. Absolutely stupid. He should refuse. He wanted to refuse. His professors, his friends, every logical part of his brain screamed stranger danger. And yet—

His hand brushed against his pocket, where the red azalea charm Cyrene had given him rested. Warmth seemed to pulse from it, almost like a heartbeat. A reminder of trust, of fate, of something beyond logic. It gave him comfort, made the tightness in his chest loosen, if only a little.

Phainon exhaled slowly. “Uh… sure,” he finally murmured, rubbing the back of his neck awkwardly. “But I don’t have any ingredients.”

The words tumbled out before he could stop them, and he immediately regretted how they sounded—like a flustered excuse, like an invitation reluctantly blurted.

Mydei only leaned in closer, his smirk deepening as though he had expected this answer all along. The proximity made Phainon’s breath hitch again. In the shifting morning light streaming through the tall library windows, Mydei looked devastatingly handsome—his sharp features softened only slightly by the glow, his golden eyes carrying that impossible weight.

Phainon’s head spun, and he tore his gaze away, pretending to busy himself with his laptop. “Don’t… don’t get too close, people are staring,” he muttered under his breath, though his pulse was hammering for reasons that had nothing to do with onlookers.

“Come on, Deliverer, why are you getting all shy? I know you’re more shameless than this,” Mydei teased, his voice pitched low enough to carry that smug lilt. Before Phainon could protest, Mydei’s hand slid into his— firm, deliberate, as though it was the most natural thing in the world.

Phainon froze, his mind blanking. Then came the coughing, awkward and stuttering, like his body was scrambling to disguise the heat rushing up his neck. Deliverer? His brain latched onto the word like a lifeline. How does he even know that nickname? Did Cyrene—

He dared not finish the thought. Instead, with all the grace of someone fleeing a battlefield, he stuffed his laptop into his bag and practically yanked Mydei to his feet. “Let’s go,” he muttered, too fast, too sharp, and dragged him toward the exit.

The scrape of chairs, the faint tuts from nearby tables, and the librarian’s warning glance followed them. Phainon’s ears burned hotter. He kept his eyes fixed on the floor tiles, striding with enough urgency to seem almost ridiculous, yet Mydei never once pulled back. Instead, Mydei let himself be tugged along, his grip steady, his expression annoyingly amused.

By the time they spilled out of the library doors and into the open air, Phainon was panting lightly, strands of hair sticking to his temples. “Do you always attract this much attention?” he asked between breaths, trying for exasperation but failing—the words landed softer, more breathless than intended.

“Hey, I’m not the one wearing purple leopard prints with yellow.” Mydei’s reply came instantly, eyes glinting as he gave Phainon’s outfit a once-over with exaggerated disdain.

Phainon’s jaw dropped. “Excuse me?!” He spun toward him, ready to fire back with a scathing comeback—until he realized.

Their hands.

Still joined, still warm, still fitting together in a way that shouldn’t have felt so natural after barely an hour of knowing each other. For a fleeting second, time seemed to still around them—the way Mydei’s thumb brushed ever so slightly against the back of his hand, the casual tilt of his head, the smile that seemed less mocking now, softer, like he was enjoying this closeness more than he let on.

Phainon’s heart lurched. He yanked his hand back as though burned, quickly turning his face away to hide the flush crawling up his cheeks. “...Touché,” he muttered, his voice clipped and uneven.

Mydei tilted his head, watching him with a smile that was far too knowing, far too patient. “You’re fun when you’re flustered,” he said lightly, but his gaze lingered, golden and unshakable, as though he saw more than Phainon wanted him to.

Phainon could only sigh in defeat as Mydei continuously teased him on their way back to the apartment.
