“Nice home.” Mydei remarked as soon as they stepped into the penthouse. His tone was casual, but his golden eyes lingered on every corner of the space with an ease that made Phainon’s stomach twist.

The two of them carried the grocery bags into the kitchen, the polished black marble under their feet reflecting the faint light from the chandeliers above. The streaks of gold in the stone gleamed faintly, almost as if the whole place was quietly showing off. Phainon busied himself unloading vegetables and pasta onto the counter, trying to ignore the way Mydei seemed far too comfortable standing there, like he already belonged.

“Thanks,” Phainon muttered when Mydei complimented the place, rubbing at the back of his neck. “But it’s actually just a rental. Some mystery rich guy owns it—I just got lucky snagging the lease.”

Mydei leaned against the counter, smirk tugging at the corner of his lips. “Mystery rich guy, huh? Yeah, that’d be me.”

Phainon froze, halfway through pulling out a packet of mushrooms. “… What?”

“I said,” Mydei drawled, tilting his head, “I’m the actual owner.”

Phainon blinked at him. Once. Twice. “That’s… that’s not even funny. Do you expect me to believe that?”

“Believe it or don’t.” Mydei shrugged, unbothered, slipping his hands into his pockets as though the conversation was already over.

And then—padding footsteps. A familiar soft mewl.

Phainon turned just in time to see Meowy, his calico, trotting across the marble floor. She ignored him entirely and went straight to Mydei, winding between his legs and pressing her head against his shin with all the possessiveness of a cat greeting her true owner.

Phainon’s jaw dropped. “Meowy?!” His voice cracked. He had never seen her warm up to a stranger that quickly, let alone look this attached.

“She’s mine,” Mydei said simply, crouching down to scratch the calico under her chin. The cat purred instantly, melting under his touch. “Thanks for taking care of her, though. Looks like you did a good job.”

Phainon stared at the scene as if the floor might suddenly collapse beneath him. His brain scrambled, trying to stitch the pieces together: the apartment, the cat, the man now making himself at home in what he thought was his home.

“…You’ve got to be kidding me. Did Cyrene know about this?” Phainon finally blurted out, clutching the counter like it could keep him grounded. “Did she set this up? Is that why she was so insistent I take this place? Because you—because this was yours all along?”

“Maybe,” Mydei said, with infuriating calm. He didn’t even glance up, continuing to pet the calico, whose purrs were growing louder by the second. “Or maybe I just… knew where you’d end up.”

“You knew?!”

“Relax, Deliverer.” Mydei finally looked up at him then, gaze steady, weighty, carrying an unreadable depth. “Everything’s exactly where it needs to be. Including you.”

Phainon’s head spun. Every coincidence—the charm, the sudden meeting, the apartment, now the cat—stacked up until he couldn’t tell whether he was living in a stroke of insane luck, or if something far stranger was moving the pieces of his life without him noticing.

And Mydei just stood there, perfectly at ease in his kitchen, like he’d been waiting for this moment all along.

“… Why are you just standing there? Don’t you have to finish your thesis?”

Phainon blinked, Mydei’s words snapping him out of his daze. “Yeah, right. I’ll be in the living room.” He retreated with his laptop, but not before stealing one last glance at the man now comfortably humming as he unpacked the groceries.

By the time Phainon was done with the final tweaks and—at long last—hit submit, the savory aroma of grilled meat had already filled the apartment. It drifted through the halls and into every corner, warm and inviting, carrying hints of smoke, rosemary, and char. His stomach growled in protest at being ignored so long.

Shutting his laptop with a satisfied thud, Phainon stretched, a wave of relief washing over him. Finally free. And as if that freedom was embodied in scent alone, the fragrance of food pulled him straight to the balcony.

What he found made him pause at the doorway.

The glass table had been transformed into something that looked like it belonged in a glossy magazine spread. There was souvlaki steak sliced and glistening, its juices still faintly steaming against the crisp September air. Roasted vegetables had been arranged with surprising care—zucchini, peppers, and aubergines caramelized at the edges, their colors vivid. Perfectly grilled mushrooms were stacked neatly on one side, their smoky richness carrying on the breeze. A basket of warm bread sat at the center, its crust golden, paired with shining bowls of dips and sauces that caught the light like little jewels.

And somehow, Mydei had even found time for dessert. A small strawberry cheesecake gleamed beneath a delicate sheen of glaze, crowned with fresh berries. Beside it, two tall glasses of milkshake waited—swirled pink, their surface frothy and sparkling faintly in the sun. The scent of pomegranate rose from them, heady and sweet, unlike anything Phainon had tasted before.

Phainon swallowed, not sure if it was his hunger or his awe that made his chest tighten. “You… you cooked all this?”

Mydei, seated casually at the table with the calico sprawled lazily across his lap, lifted his gaze with a smirk. “What did you expect? I said I’d cook, didn’t I?” He slid one of the milkshakes across the table with a flick of his wrist. “Sit down, Deliverer. You’ve earned this meal after surviving a year of school.”

Phainon’s pulse quickened at the word Deliverer, the strange weight it carried pressing against the edges of his chest, but he obeyed, almost dazed. He took his seat across from Mydei, though his eyes lingered more on the man than the feast before him. Mydei looked utterly at ease, sunlight gilding the sharp line of his jaw, his posture relaxed as if this was his balcony, his table, his home—like he had always belonged here.

Phainon reached for the fork and cut into the steak, bringing the first bite to his lips. The moment it touched his tongue, his chest tightened. Flavor burst across his senses—smoky, savory, tender, with herbs that reminded him of a childhood long blurred at the edges. He had eaten at fine restaurants before, tasted the so-called best cuisines the world could offer, but this… this was different. This was warmth. Comfort. Home.

His throat bobbed as he swallowed, his eyes stinging unexpectedly. He quickly hid the tremor in his voice with a low hum. “Did Cyrene put you up to this?” he asked, chewing slowly, savoring.

Mydei tilted his head, brow quirking. “What makes you think so?”

Phainon gestured vaguely with his fork, trying to sound casual, though his heart betrayed him by beating too fast. “It’s just… crazy to me. A stranger going this far, doing something like this. Cooking for me, making me feel like—” He paused, catching himself, then laughed softly. “I don’t know. Like I’m not a stranger to you. Don’t you think it’s… fate?”

For a heartbeat, silence stretched between them, broken only by the faint clink of cutlery and the breeze rustling the curtains.

Then, to Phainon’s surprise, Mydei chuckled. Not mocking, not careless—a low, warm laugh that softened every sharp edge of his expression. The smirk faded, replaced by something gentler, almost reverent.

“Fate, huh?” Mydei repeated, leaning back in his chair. The golden light caught in his eyes, and for the briefest moment, he looked older than he should, as though he carried entire lifetimes behind that smile. His gaze softened, solemn and fond all at once, and he nodded slowly. “… Yeah. Maybe you’re right.”

Phainon blinked, startled by the sudden tenderness in his tone. He hadn’t expected agreement, much less the way Mydei said it—as though he wasn’t talking about possibility, but inevitability. A quiet certainty.

The weight of it made Phainon’s chest swell and ache in equal measure. He dropped his gaze to his plate, hoping Mydei hadn’t noticed how his ears had gone red.

Across the table, Mydei simply smiled, letting the moment linger.

The balcony air was sweet with the faint perfume of grilled herbs and roasted vegetables, the pink milkshake—that Phainon learnt was really pomegranate juice with milk—glimmering like liquid sunlight in the glasses. What was meant to be lunch slowly unraveled into hours of easy conversation.

Phainon found himself leaning across the table more often than not, drawn closer without even realizing it. At first, it was small things—an offhanded joke from Mydei that made him snort into his drink, a teasing quip that had him groaning and covering his face with his hands. But then, it shifted. They began trading stories about places they had traveled, professors they couldn’t stand, small memories that had no real weight but somehow felt precious when shared here, between them.

It was odd, Phainon thought. He didn’t usually open up this way. With most people, he needed time—days, weeks, months even—to trust them with anything personal. But with Mydei, he barely noticed the walls coming down. One moment he was awkward, trying to mask his racing heart, and the next, he was laughing freely, his shoulders relaxed, his voice unguarded.

Every so often, he would catch himself staring. At the way Mydei’s golden eyes caught the evening light. At the way his lips curved into the kind of smile that looked like it had been made only for him. At how natural it all felt, as if they weren’t strangers at all.

The sun dipped lower and lower, painting the sky in streaks of rose and violet, and Phainon nearly jolted when he realized how late it had become. The plates were nearly empty, the cat was dozing between them, and yet, he didn’t feel like moving—not from this balcony, not from this moment.

Then, Mydei leaned forward, resting his chin lazily on his hand. His gaze was steady, searching, almost too heavy for Phainon’s racing heart.

“So anyways,” Mydei began casually, like he was asking about the weather, “since you’re done with school… any chance you’d want to go to Aedes Elysiae with me for a holiday?”

Phainon blinked. “…Huh?”

Mydei’s lips quirked into that smirk again. “You heard me. A short trip. Nothing dramatic.” His tone was light, but there was an edge to his eyes, a spark of something unspoken.

Phainon let out a surprised laugh, shaking his head. “Some crazy hot guy is asking me to run away with him to my hometown? Yeah, I’ll go.”

He had meant to sound amused, but the words came out softer than expected, almost shy. And when Mydei’s expression shifted into a smile— one that wasn’t teasing, but warm, touched with something solemn— Phainon’s chest gave another painful squeeze.

And when Mydei’s expression shifted into a smile—one that wasn’t teasing, but warm, touched with something solemn—Phainon’s chest gave another painful squeeze.

“Great,” Mydei said simply, leaning back in his chair as if he had just decided the weather. “We’ll leave tomorrow.”

Phainon nearly choked on the last sip of his milkshake. “T-Tomorrow? Already? Don’t we need to, I don’t know, plan or book something? Where are we even meeting? The station? The airport?”

Mydei’s gaze flicked toward him, steady and unbothered. “No need. I’ll be staying here for the night.”

For a moment, Phainon could only blink. His brain lagged a full three seconds behind before he laughed, shaking his head as if that would dispel the sudden heat crawling up his neck. “Staying here? Wow, bold move. Why not just hop into bed with me while you’re at it?” he teased, adding a wink for good measure.

The corner of Mydei’s mouth twitched—but not in amusement. His golden eyes didn’t waver, his expression unreadably calm as he answered with a deadpan, “Sure.”

The air froze.

Phainon’s grin faltered. He stared, waiting for the smirk, for the laugh, for some sign that Mydei was joking. But there was none. Just the quiet certainty of someone who meant every word he said.

“…You’re not serious,” Phainon whispered, but his voice was already betraying him, the edges fraying with nerves.

Mydei tilted his head slightly, gaze intent, his tone still flat. “Why wouldn’t I be?”

Phainon went utterly silent, heart hammering against his ribs as he looked away, suddenly very aware of how small the distance between them felt.

What the hell had he just gotten himself into?

The train rattled softly along the tracks, its windows glowing faintly with the first light of dawn. Outside, the world was still wrapped in a pale mist, mountains and fields unfurling like brushstrokes across the horizon. Inside their carriage, the air was warm and hushed, punctuated only by the occasional murmur of other early travelers and the rhythmic hum of steel wheels.

Phainon leaned back against the seat, his travel mug of coffee nestled between his palms, stealing glances at the man beside him. Mydei sat with one leg crossed over the other, gaze fixed lazily out the window, his profile illuminated by the rising sun. He looked absurdly at ease—as if this journey was the most natural thing in the world, while Phainon’s stomach was still tangled in knots from everything that had happened yesterday.

They had already spent an hour talking about trivial things—favorite foods, books, and Phainon’s endless movie anecdotes, which Mydei tolerated with a faint smirk. Somehow, despite having met only yesterday, their banter flowed so easily that it unsettled Phainon just as much as it comforted him.

Finally, after a lull in conversation, Phainon tilted his head, narrowing his eyes. “So… Is there any reason why we’re going to Aedes Elysiae?”

Mydei didn’t answer immediately. He tapped his fingers lightly on the armrest, as though weighing how much to reveal, before finally murmuring, “It’s your hometown.”

“Yeah… but…” Phainon frowned, leaning in.

Mydei turned then, his golden eyes catching the light with a spark that made Phainon’s pulse skip. “You could introduce me to your parents.”

Phainon nearly spat out his coffee. “M-My parents?! We’ve known each other for, what, a day?” His face flushed hot as he waved his hands in front of him. “You can’t just—”

Mydei’s mouth curved into a crooked grin, enjoying the way Phainon squirmed. “Relax. I’m kidding.”

“Not funny,” Phainon muttered, still red.

But the grin faded as quickly as it had appeared, replaced by something quieter, heavier. Mydei shifted his gaze back toward the window, voice dropping low. “There’s something I want to show you.”

The words lingered, cloaked in mystery. He didn’t elaborate, and for some reason, Phainon didn’t push further. There was weight in the way Mydei said it—like he was carrying something fragile, something that couldn’t yet be spoken aloud.

Phainon studied him for a moment longer, noting the calm set of his jaw, the way his fingers had stilled against the armrest, before looking away himself. His chest tightened with a strange mix of curiosity and unease, but also a quiet thrill.

Whatever this “something” was, he had a feeling it wasn’t going to be ordinary.

As the train slowed, the gentle rocking gave way to a steadier rhythm, and Phainon pressed a palm against the glass, his breath catching at the sight beyond.

The familiar outlines of the landscape stretched before him—rolling hills painted in shades of amber-orange, dotted with cherry blossom trees that bloomed defiantly against the breeze. The petals floated lazily through the air, carried on currents that made them look almost deliberate, as though the land itself was welcoming him home.

The closer they drew, the more Phainon became aware of the charm in his shirt pocket. Cyrene’s gift—once light and unobtrusive—now pressed insistently against his chest, weighted with an unseen force. It pulsed faintly with warmth, or maybe that was just his imagination, but either way it demanded his attention, as though whispering, remember why you’re here.

He placed his hand on his chest for a moment, trying to shake the strange pull.

The cityscape of Okehema slipped further and further behind them, replaced by cobblestone streets and old-world architecture. Roofs of dark terracotta sloped low, ivy climbed up stone walls, and narrow alleyways wound like secret passages between the buildings. The transition was seamless yet startling, like stepping back through time.

When the train finally hissed to a halt and the doors opened, Phainon stepped onto the platform and inhaled deeply. The air was crisp and cool, carrying the heady mingling of pine and flowers. It wasn’t just the scent of spring—it was the scent of home. His throat tightened unexpectedly, nostalgia flooding him so suddenly he had to blink hard to steady himself.

The square outside the station unfolded like a memory reborn. Merchants were setting up their stalls, their carts laden with oranges, olives, and fresh bread still steaming from the ovens. The sound of a distant lute drifted faintly through the streets, mingling with the chatter of civilians greeting one another. Everything about it felt impossibly familiar—down to the rhythm of footsteps on stone, the gentle creak of wooden shutters, the laughter echoing in narrow passageways.

Yet as Phainon stood there, soaking it all in, a strange unease wove through his chest. It wasn’t just nostalgia. It was something else—something deeper, like he had stood in this exact moment before, down to the weight of the charm against his skin and the warmth of the sunlight on his face.

He caught himself shivering, though the air wasn’t cold.

Beside him, Mydei adjusted the strap of his bag and cast Phainon a sidelong glance. His expression was unreadable—too calm, too deliberate, as if he were waiting for something.

Phainon tore his gaze from the town and forced a laugh, running a hand through his hair. “Sorry, it’s been awhile since I’ve been here. I was just… remembering something.”

But even as he said it, he couldn’t shake the sense that this was more than just nostalgia. That he was walking into a memory he couldn’t quite recall —one that Mydei already seemed to know.

Mydei said nothing and simply took his hand, tugging him toward the nearest taxi stand with a quiet certainty that left no room for questions.

Phainon followed, though his chest felt tight with confusion. He hadn’t told Mydei anything—not the name of his village, not where he had grown up, not even vague directions. And yet, Mydei leaned casually into the driver’s window and gave the exact address without hesitation, his voice steady, like he had always known.

Phainon’s brows knitted as he slid into the back seat beside him. His first thought, instinctively, was Cyrene. Had she told Mydei? Was this another one of her strange games, weaving coincidences into inevitabilities? He wanted to ask outright, but each time he opened his mouth, Mydei’s calm presence pressed the words back down into silence.

The taxi ride was long, the scenery shifting gradually from bustling town squares into open fields. Phainon’s heart pounded harder the closer they came, the familiar smell of wheat and wildflowers creeping in through the cracked windows. Fields of golden stalks stretched out endlessly, swaying gently with the spring breeze like waves of sunlight. Narrow cobbled roads wound between them, leading toward clusters of homes—small, stone cottages with tiled roofs weathered by time, ivy clinging to their walls like old memories. Flowerbeds spilled over low fences, filled with tulips and lilies that turned their heads toward the afternoon sun.

When the taxi finally slowed, Phainon’s breath caught in his throat. He knew this place. He knew it. Every curve of the road, every shade of the stones beneath his feet, every scent carried on the breeze—it was his village. Home.

For a moment, his knees felt weak. He turned toward Mydei, questions burning at the tip of his tongue—How do you know this place? Why bring me here?—but Mydei only offered him a glance, his eyes calm yet unreadable, and then stepped out of the cab without a word.

Phainon followed, his heart hammering as Mydei took his hand again, his grip firm and unyielding, guiding him down the cobbled path. The silence between them pressed heavier than words could.

They reached the village’s main plaza, and before Phainon could gather his thoughts, the air shifted. The low chatter of merchants and townsfolk stopped as heads began to turn. One by one, the villagers froze where they stood, their gazes fixed on him. Their expressions were a mixture of surprise and recognition—like seeing a face they hadn’t expected to return, yet had always hoped for.

“Phainon?” a voice whispered from the crowd, breaking the stillness.

And suddenly, the quiet plaza seemed to breathe. The murmurs grew louder, swelling into something warm and overwhelming as people began to approach, their faces alight with familiarity. Phainon stood rooted to the spot, overwhelmed, the weight of their recognition sinking deep into his chest.

But all the while, Mydei stood just behind him, silent and steady, his hand still joined with Phainon’s as if he had never once doubted that this was exactly where they were meant to be. Phainon awkwardly lifted his free hand in a half-hearted wave, muttering a soft, “Hi,” as the villagers pressed in with greetings, pats on the back, and cries of welcome. He could feel his ears burning as one too many people exclaimed about how tall he had grown, or how much he looked like his father.

Through it all, Mydei made absolutely no move to let go of his hand. If anything, his grip tightened whenever Phainon shifted, as though reminding him silently: don’t even think about wriggling away. It was infuriating, and —if he was honest with himself—a little comforting.

But all traces of composure vanished the moment his parents broke through the crowd.

“Phainon!” Hieronymus boomed, sweeping his son into a crushing hug that nearly lifted him off his feet. “You should have told us you were coming— we would have prepared a feast! The whole village would’ve celebrated!”

“Dad, I—ack—can’t breathe!” Phainon sputtered, prying himself free only to be caught by his mother next.

“Phainon, dear!” Audata fussed, brushing his hair back from his face as though he were still ten years old. “You’ve lost weight, haven’t you? Are you eating properly in that big city?”

“Mom, please—”

And then her gaze shifted, her eyes twinkling as they landed on Mydei. “Ohhh. And who is this? Is he your boyfriend? He’s very handsome.”

Phainon nearly choked on air. “Wh—Mom!”

Before he could protest, Mydei inclined his head smoothly, his voice calm and warm: “Thank you, ma’am. You’re beautiful as well.”

Audata flushed, clasping her hands together. “Oh, and he’s polite too!”

Phainon’s jaw dropped. “Hold on, wait—he’s not—”

“Yes,” Mydei cut in, tone infuriatingly steady. “I’m his.”

The villagers nearby tittered, his mother beamed like the sun, and his father clapped Mydei on the shoulder with an approving grin. “Good! About time our boy brought someone respectable home.”

Phainon, caught in the middle of the circus, looked like he might spontaneously combust. His ears were crimson, his words tripping uselessly over one another as he tried to backpedal. “I—he—we’re not—Mydei!”

But Mydei only gave him that insufferably smug little smirk, his thumb brushing ever so casually over the back of Phainon’s hand as though sealing the deal. Every expression, every word out of his mouth, made it obvious: everything was unfolding exactly the way he wanted.

And Phainon, helpless in the whirlwind of his parents’ delight and Mydei’s maddening composure, could only sulk, looking like a kicked puppy as everyone continued to tease him.

Thankfully, after a gruelling ten minutes of being paraded around like some prized heir returning from a war, Mydei finally came to his rescue. With a smooth smile and a few well-chosen words, he excused them both from the endless barrage of questions, promising they’d be back in time for the feast that evening.

Phainon shot him a grateful glare—one that was meant to say “You started this”—but Mydei only smirked knowingly, as if to say “And I ended it too.”

They dropped off their belongings at a quaint little cottage at the edge of the village. The place was small but cozy, with ivy creeping along its stone walls and the soft fragrance of wildflowers drifting through the open windows. Phainon barely had time to catch his breath before Mydei tugged gently at his wrist, guiding him back outside.

“Come on,” he said, voice lighter than usual. “There’s something I want to show you.”

The path they took wound through narrow cobbled lanes and fields of swaying wheat, until the terrain began to change—stone ruins appeared here and there, half-swallowed by moss and vines, relics of an older time. And then, at the crest of a gentle hill, they arrived.

The old chapel stood in silence, a solemn relic of a forgotten age. Time had not been kind to it: ivy crawled up its once-proud walls, and most of the roof had long since crumbled away, leaving only a jagged skeleton through which shafts of afternoon sunlight poured like golden spears. Where stained glass windows once glimmered, now only fractured shards remained, their colors faint but still catching the light in ghostly hues of crimson, cobalt, and violet.

The air inside was cool and still, filled with the faint scent of old stone and earth. And at its heart—half-shrouded in shadow—stood the statue of Oronyx. It was enormous, rising almost to what remained of the ceiling, yet faceless and weathered by centuries. Only the outline of its broad shoulders and legs remained intact. Moss had crept into its cracks, azalea flowers bloomed at its base.

Phainon stood frozen at the threshold. Despite the ruin and neglect, the place felt sacred—holy, even. It was as though time itself had stopped here, as though the chapel had been waiting patiently for someone to return.

“This place…” he breathed, his voice barely a whisper. “I used to come here as a kid.”

Mydei stepped past him, his footsteps soft against the cracked stone floor. “I know.”

“You know?” Phainon blinked, turning to look at him.

But Mydei didn’t answer. He was standing before the faceless statue now, his expression unreadable, bathed in the fractured light pouring through the roof. The silence stretched between them, heavy and ancient, like the chapel itself.

There was something in the way Mydei looked at the statue—something reverent, almost sorrowful. And though Phainon couldn’t explain it, a strange sensation stirred in his chest.

He couldn’t shake the feeling that he had been here before. With him.

Mydei gently tugged on their joined hands, drawing Phainon closer to the towering statue. The weight of the silence pressed down on them, broken only by the soft shuffle of their footsteps echoing against the stone floor.

At the statue’s base, half-hidden by moss and age, was a small square recess —too precise to be natural, too deliberate to be accidental. A keyhole, carved into the ancient stone.

“Do you have your charm with you?” Mydei asked, voice quiet but steady.

Phainon blinked, confused by the sudden question, but nodded nonetheless. He slipped his hand into his chest pocket, the familiar weight of the red azalea charm warm against his palm. When he brought it out, the sunlight filtering through the broken roof caught on its casing, setting the crimson petals aglow.

Then, to his utter surprise, Mydei reached into his own pocket and produced another charm—one that mirrored Phainon’s in every way except one. The flower within was blue.

Phainon’s breath caught. Cyrene’s words surfaced unbidden in his mind, echoing like a distant memory: “If you ever see a blue azalea, hold on to it forever.”

Before he could voice the sudden flurry of questions rising in his chest, Mydei was already moving. Wordlessly, he guided Phainon’s hand toward the recess, fitting the red charm into one side of the keyhole with practiced ease. Then he did the same with the blue, slotting it into the opposite end.

The air shifted.

With a deep, ancient groan, the stone beneath their feet trembled. Dust rained down from the cracks in the ceiling as the base of the statue began to move—slowly, heavily—like a beast rousing from centuries of slumber. A seam split open along the floor, revealing a hidden compartment that had been sealed for gods knew how long.

Phainon’s heartbeat thundered in his ears. He turned to Mydei, but the other man only watched him silently, his golden eyes gleaming with a mixture of anticipation and something far deeper.

“Go on,” Mydei murmured. “Look.”

With hesitant fingers, Phainon crouched down and peered into the compartment. Inside was a single object, resting in the hollow like a relic of another age.

A book.

It was in pristine condition, completely untouched by time. This was the first time he had seen this book and yet, the moment Phainon’s eyes landed on it, something in his chest lurched. The sight of it—it was familiar.

His fingers trembled as he reached out to touch it, a shiver racing down his spine the moment his skin brushed the surface.

“I…” His voice caught. “I’ve seen this before.”

Mydei said nothing. But when Phainon looked up, he found those golden eyes fixed on him with such intensity it was almost overwhelming. There was weight in Mydei’s gaze—like he was watching a moment centuries in the making unfold before him.

And though Phainon didn’t understand, though his mind was a storm of confusion, a single, unshakable truth settled somewhere deep in his bones.

This—whatever this was—wasn’t the first time.

It felt as though he had stood in this very place before, his hand hovering over this very book.

And for the first time, the word fate no longer felt like a joke.

Phainon hesitated, the weight of the book grounding him and yet calling him forward all at once. It was heavy — not just in its physicality, but in presence, in purpose. As if something ancient and inevitable pulsed beneath its shining blue and gold cover, waiting for him to lift the veil.

He swallowed hard and opened it.

The world exploded.

A blinding light burst forth from between the pages — not warm and golden, but searing and white, too bright to be earthly. It enveloped the room, swallowed the chapel, swallowed him. Phainon gasped, stumbling backward as the ground beneath his feet dissolved into nothingness.

Then the memories came.

Not one by one — but all at once.

They crashed into him like a tidal wave, a storm too vast for his mind to contain. Faces, places, voices. The sound of laughter. The taste of tears. The weight of battles fought, lives lived and lost. He saw himself — over and over again — in a thousand different lives, a thousand different deaths. And always, always, him.

Mydei.

The name reverberated through the flood, anchoring it all. Phainon’s breath hitched as the visions sharpened, showing him not dreams but truths.

The world of Amphoreus, breaking and reforming, again and again. Thirty-three million cycles, countless iterations of the same beginning and end. And at the heart of every rebirth stood Mydei, reaching for him through the chaos.

The first time they met. The first time they fought side by side. The first time they kissed. The first time they swore they would find each other again. And the previous cycle where he had been once again cursed with the same fate even in a different world.

His heart seized as he felt it — the moment he was knocked out. One moment he had held Mydei in his arms and the next moment, he was out cold. That final scene had been a blur to him as well. He wasn’t sure if had actually died or not.

But the pages turned themselves, showing him what came after.

A memory Phainon had never lived.

It unfolded before his eyes like a film cast upon the fabric of his mind — foreign and yet deeply familiar. After he had collapsed, Mydei had taken the book and vanished into the cold twilight streets of Castrum Kremnos. He walked with purpose, alone beneath the sickly glow of the lamplights, until he reached a small, unremarkable house at the city’s edge — the one that smelled faintly of cedar and rain. It was there, in that room that used to be Phainon’s study, that the impossible was decided.

Phainon felt the weight of it long before he understood what was happening. The air inside the house was thick, charged with a kind of gravity that pressed against his chest. Mydei stood before an open window, the night breeze ruffling his hair, while Cyrene sat by a worn oak table, her expression carved from stone. There was no hesitation in either of them — only resignation, and an understanding of the terrible balance that governed their world.

Rewriting fate required a price. A greater wish demanded a heavier sacrifice. It was an immutable law — one Mydei accepted without protest.

And so, he made his decision.

The memories came to Phainon, vivid and raw: the tremor in Mydei’s hands as he opened the book, the hollow ache in his chest as he prepared to carve away everything he was. He would relinquish his name, his lineage, his past. The prince of Castrum Kremnos, the heir to Chrysos, would vanish from the pages of history. He would not exist — not as a noble, not as a demigod, not even as a fragment of someone’s memory.

He would become nobody.

And in doing so, he would unmake the cycle itself. The so-called Creator — Zandar, the architect of Amphoreus — would be cast down from his pedestal. No longer omnipotent, no longer omniscient. He would awaken as an ordinary human, stripped of his power, ignorant of the loops and laws he had once governed.

Phainon saw the ink flow across the parchment like blood. He felt the world tilt, warp, and shudder as reality bent under the weight of Mydei’s will. And then — light. A soundless explosion of radiance swallowed everything whole.

When the world reassembled, it was no longer the same.

Mydei awoke in a field bathed in dawn’s pale glow, his body heavy and disoriented, as though he had been born anew. The grass was cool against his skin, damp with morning dew, and the scent of mountain laurel clung to the air. In the distance, rooftops of terracotta and white stone peeked through a veil of mist — Aedes Elysiae.

The memories surged behind his eyes — a storm of thirty-three million lifetimes, each one burning with the sound of Phainon’s laughter, the warmth of his touch, the ache of his absence. Mydei clutched at his chest, trembling beneath the weight of everything he still remembered.

And then, footsteps.

A figure approached slowly, their silhouette framed by the morning light. It was Cyrene. Her unmistakable pink hair caught the breeze, her eyes calm and unknowing. A young budding actress who was currently visiting Aedes Elysiae during her vacation.

She spoke, though the words were distant and hollow — polite curiosity from a stranger’s lips. There was no recognition in her gaze. No history. No shared scars.

She did not know him.

And neither did the world. Zandar lived somewhere now as a mortal man, blissfully unaware of the power he once wielded. Mydei himself was nothing more than a name — a shadow wandering through a rewritten reality.

It was the price he had chosen. The weight he had sworn to bear.

But as he accepted Cyrene’s outstretched hand and let her pull him to his feet, a single truth remained bright and unbroken amid the ruin of all he had surrendered:

Phainon was still out there.

And this time, no cycle, no destiny, no titan would keep them apart.

Through the haze of light and fractured visions, another thread of the past unraveled — slower this time, gentler, like the turning of a fragile page.

The scene shifted to a sunlit veranda overlooking the wheat fields of Aedes Elysiae. Mydei sat opposite her at a weathered table, his expression calm yet determined. Words passed between them — fragments that Phainon couldn’t quite hear — but he knew what they were about. Cyrene’s brows furrowed slightly, confusion flickering in her gaze as Mydei spoke of events that she did not remember, bonds that to her had never existed.

“Phainon,” Mydei said again — and this time, she stilled. Something had shifted, some distant bell in her mind that had never rung before. Slowly, with hesitant fingers, she reached into her satchel and pulled out a charm — a small pink azalea pendant that shimmered faintly under the sunlight.

Phainon’s heart clenched.

She explained — or rather, remembered — that she had once heard of relics like these. That if used correctly, they could hold pieces of memory within them. Even fragments of lives once lived.

Mydei’s eyes widened. He reached instinctively into his pocket and found two charms resting there — one red, one blue — the same as before. And as his gaze fell upon them, something shifted in the air around them.

Recognition.

Cyrene inhaled sharply, her hand flying to her mouth as if struck by something too vast for words. The confusion melted from her expression, replaced by dawning awareness — not full memory, not yet, but the unmistakable pull of something real. Something true.

A plan began to form in her eyes — one that promised she could help him find what he was searching for. What they were searching for.

And then — the vision shattered.

The flood of images broke apart like glass, and the world lurched back into motion. Phainon gasped, stumbling backward as the last traces of the memory bled away. The chapel’s ruined ceiling came back into focus, the fractured statue of Oronyx looming above him, the scent of dust and age pressing against his lungs.

And before him stood Mydei — the same Mydei who had erased himself from history, who had wandered lifetimes just to find him again.

It was too much — far too much.

Phainon’s breath hitched. All the weight of thirty-three million cycles, all the ache and longing, all the empty years — it came crashing down on him in a single, uncontrollable wave. Somewhere beneath the chaos, beneath the grief and awe and disbelief, a single, undeniable truth began to take root.

He had always known Mydei.

He had always loved him.

And Mydei… had never once stopped loving him back.

The chapel around him slowly came back into focus, the blinding light fading into a soft, warm glow. Phainon was trembling, tears streaming down his cheeks, the book still open in his hands.

He moved before he could think, before he could even speak. His body acted on its own, surging forward and throwing itself into Mydei’s arms.

The impact was desperate. Messy. Unrestrained.

Phainon buried his face into Mydei’s shoulder and broke.

“I missed you—” The words were half-sob, half-laughter, raw and trembling. “I missed you so much…”

His hands fisted in the back of Mydei’s shirt, holding on as though the world might tear them apart again if he let go. His chest heaved with sobs that shook through him, uncontrollable, years of grief and confusion finally given a voice.

And Mydei — for once — said nothing. He simply held him, steady and warm, one hand cradling the back of Phainon’s head, the other pressed firmly against his spine, anchoring him in place.

For the first time in countless cycles, they were no longer separated by fate, or time, or memory. There was nobody who could come between them anymore.

For the first time, they were home.

For Mydei, readjusting to life was… difficult. Far more difficult than he had expected. The world he had rewritten was kind and bright — but it was also alien, stripped of the things that had once defined him.

There were mornings when he woke up and instinctively reached for a name that no longer belonged to him. Afternoons when he walked through the marble streets of Castrum Kremnos and caught glimpses of familiar faces who, for the first time in centuries, did not know who he was. People he had bled for. Fought beside. Loved. Now, they were strangers.

His mother still tended to the gardens in the imperial courtyard, laughing as she always did. His father still rode with the king’s guard. And their son — their son — was now a young man named Hephaestion, well on his way to becoming a great ruler of Castrum Kremnos.

Sometimes, Mydei would linger across the street just to watch them. Never close enough to be noticed, never foolish enough to reach out. It ached — titans, it ached — to know that his place at their table had been rewritten, his very existence excised from their story. But if they were alive… if they were happy… that was enough.

There were others too. Old friends who greeted him with polite smiles, unaware that they once shared battlefields and dreams. Neighbours who spoke to him like a stranger. People he had sworn to protect who now passed him by without recognition. Each encounter left a hollow ache in his chest, a bittersweet reminder of the price he had paid.

And then there was Zandar.

Mydei never spoke of that day — not to Phainon, not to Cyrene, not to anyone. All Cyrene knew was that he had gone to visit the so-called “creator” not long after the new timeline had begun. The rest… was history. Whatever happened behind those closed doors, Zandar never returned to the public eye again.

Still, amidst the hollow spaces and quiet grief, there were moments of light. Cyrene, as she often did, became his anchor. She had extended a hand to him when he had none to grasp — offering a place in Chrysos, her company, and coaxing him to be the guitarist for their performers. Later on, Cerydra had decided to allow him to debut as an independent artist due to his talent. The music, at least, was familiar. It reminded him that he was still capable of creating beauty.

As for the Chrysos Heirs…

Phainon and Mydei had agreed — without ever needing to say it aloud — that the past would remain theirs alone. The cycles, the flamechase, the rewritten fate, all of it… it was a truth too heavy to share. This world was supposed to be a fresh start, so they decided to treat it as one.

Naturally, that meant they also needed a believable story about how they’d met. It wasn’t hard to piece one together — something about a chance encounter at a music bar and a mutual love for terrible reality TV. It was simple enough, though their friends clearly weren’t buying every word of it.

The news of their relationship had shocked everyone. And perhaps “shocked” was an understatement.

“Mydei? This Mydei?” Hyacine asked for the third time that afternoon, squinting at him like she was inspecting a rare animal. “How’d you even pull a baddie like this? The Phainon I know has absolutely no rizz.”

“Hyacine!” Phainon spluttered, cheeks burning scarlet as laughter rippled through the café.

Mydei, meanwhile, was trying very hard not to cringe. “Rizz,” as he had learned, was apparently a word now — one of many modern slang terms that made him feel like an ancient relic masquerading as a twenty-something.

Still, watching them bicker filled his chest with something warm. These faces — Hyacine, Cipher, everyone else — were the same ones he had fought beside and laughed with in another life. They didn’t remember him, and yet, somehow, it still felt like coming home.

“I’ll have you know,” Phainon said proudly, puffing up his chest, “that I charmed him with my charismatic personality and my handsome face!”

“Don’t listen to him,” Mydei interrupted smoothly, leaning back in his seat with a smug grin. “He was literally obsessed with me. Begging me to be his boyfriend.”

“I— that’s not how it happened!” Phainon shot back, nearly knocking over his drink.

“Titans, do you two ever stop flirting?” Cipher groaned, burying her face in her hands. “It’s like watching a drama unfold in real-time.”

“Oh, let them be,” March teased, snapping a photo of the two with her phone. “I never thought we’d live to see the day Phainon gets a boyfriend, let alone one who looks like that.”

Mydei couldn’t help but laugh — genuinely laugh — at their antics. It was easy to slip into the rhythm of their group, even if they didn’t remember the battles they’d once shared or the lifetimes they had survived together. This was a new beginning.

And for the first time, he wasn’t watching from the sidelines. He was part of their world again — not as a prince, not as a savior, not as a name carved into history. Just as Mydei.

And finally, there was Phainon.

Always Phainon.

Phainon, who thanked Cyrene endlessly despite her playful insistence that she “didn’t do anything.” Phainon, who made Mydei laugh again. Who reached for his hand without hesitation. Who spoke to him not as a prince or a savior, but simply as Mydei.

When night fell on a casual Wednesday, the quiet of their shared home wrapped around them like a comforting blanket. The city lights beyond the balcony windows blinked faintly, distant and hazy, and the only sounds were the soft rustle of sheets and the muted rhythm of their breathing. It was the kind of stillness that felt rare — the kind that settled deep in one’s bones.

They lay facing each other in bed, the world dim and warm around them. Phainon had one arm tucked beneath his pillow, his silver hair falling messily into his eyes, while Mydei rested on his side, an arm draped loosely around Phainon’s waist. The calico cat had already claimed its usual spot at the foot of the bed, curled into a soft ball of fur.

For a long while, neither spoke. They didn’t need to — the silence between them wasn’t empty. It was filled with everything they didn’t have to say: the memories they now shared, the lives they had lived, and the future they were quietly building together.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon said suddenly, his voice breaking the hush of the room.

Mydei’s golden eyes flickered open, warm and unguarded as they found Phainon’s. “What is it, Deliverer?” he murmured, his tone soft and sleepy, as though the name itself was a lullaby.

Phainon didn’t answer right away. He just stared at him, drinking in every detail — the curve of his jaw, the faint freckles that dusted his cheeks, the gentle rise and fall of his chest. So many times before, they had been torn apart by circumstance, by time, by fate itself. And yet, here he was now. Real. Tangible. His.

“I love you,” Phainon said simply. There was no fanfare, no elaborate speech. Just three words, quiet but heavy, carrying the weight of thirty-three million cycles, a thousand lifetimes, and countless sacrifices.

For a heartbeat, Mydei didn’t speak. He only stared, his expression softening with something deeper than words could hold. His fingers reached out, brushing gently against Phainon’s cheek — a touch so light it was almost reverent — before he leaned in, pressing their foreheads together.

“I love you too,” he whispered, his voice barely above a breath. But the words thrummed with certainty, with a promise that reached beyond this moment, beyond this life.

They stayed like that, eyes half-lidded, foreheads pressed together, as the night stretched on. And for the first time in what felt like eternity, neither of them worried about what tomorrow would bring. All that mattered was this — the steady beat of a heart against their own, the warmth of a hand they never thought they’d hold again.

It was simple. It was quiet. And yet, it meant everything.

The world Mydei had rewritten wasn’t perfect — it never would be. But as he watched Phainon fall asleep beside him one quiet evening, fingers loosely tangled together, he felt no regret.

Every sacrifice — every memory, every name, every piece of himself he had cast away — had been worth it.
